div.head: WARRItIGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRItIGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
THE COUNTY COUNCIL'S " IMPERTINENCE."
Wilderspool Causeway Improvement.
LIVELY DEBATE.

The municipal year was brought to a close with a meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided and there were also present :—The Deputy Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Aldermen A Bennett, John Eaans, James Evans, W Pierpoint and .1 Smethurst; Councillors 0 Archer, T H Ashcroft, T Dirties, T Chantler, J 0 Crsik, E Cnoninston, .1 Dickenson, J tinniest!, J Hawthorn. R Henshall, C Jackson Holmes, W II .1 Jenkins, F T Lnahford, J T Locker, Dr McKee, J Pembertoo, H Roberts, W Rogers, J Skeliend, 0 Toole, J Wilkinson, and W J Wilson ; Messrs J Lyon Whittle(town clerk), A Hallman, (deputy Town Clerk), J Fsirhnrst (borough treasurer), T Longdin (borough surveyor), C Madeley (librarian), W S Haddock (gas engineer). F V L Mathias (electrical engineer), J H Murray (director of education, Dr J C ilibbert (medical allcer), and .1 Gray :.water engineer). CONGRATULATIONS.
The MAYOR offered his congratulations to those retiring councillors who had that day teen returned unopposed. (Hear, hear).

- • • SPECIAL CONSTABLES. The minutes of the Watch Committee, which were confirmed, showed that the Chief Constable suggested that each special constable should be supplied with a staff and armlet as a memento of his services during the recent strike. The matter was left in the hands of the Mayor and Chief Constable.—The Chief Constable reported upon the proceedings of n conference convened by the Manchester Watch Committee on the Home Office circular referring to the appointment of special constables. Alderman BEMNELT said that in some towns a per- meet organization had already been established for those who were willing in times of emergency to devote themselves to civic service. had any steps been taken in Warrington? The 151, \OR : The matter is under consider- ation now.
The minutes were approved. WILDERSPOOL IMPROVEMENT. COUNCIL PAILS TO ACQUIRE PROPERTY. SPIRITED CRITICISM.

When the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee were submitted, Councillor ROBRRTS said he felt it his duty to call public attention to the resolution authorizing the Town Clerk to offer a sum not exceeding £250 for the purchase of the premises No. 28 and 30, Wilderspool- causeway, which bad been in the market. He said that not long ago the Council discursed the desirability of making some provision for the safety of the public by the removal of certain property and the con- struction of a street between River-road and the (Surewny. They were then told by the Chair- man of the Street Improvement Committee—he believed In perfect good faith—that it was the intention of ths committee et the earliest opportunity to acquire he properties which formed the keystone of the mprovement and which were offered for sale last week. Yet the committee passed a resolution restricting the Town Clerk to an offer of .C 250 for property which was the very apex of the trianglikand which would hsve to come down sooner or later. It was extremely regrettable that, with a knowledge of the value of property in the district, they should hive taken such a step. The first lid at the sale was £3(O and eventually the property changed handset .C 350. In order to effect an improvement which everybody in the Council who was not blinded by prejudice admitted wee essential, they would have to buy the property from the new owner at some price in excess of £530. Until they could secure it by private treaty, the scheme Woad be delayed. He could not see any defence tz the action of the committee. Alderman Brorrrr said he agreed with Councillor Roberts that the committee was absolutely wrong in the course it had adopted. If any member. whited to defend their lotion they were at liberty to do no. Alderman SNIP:TM:Ref said he could not Ind words to exprees his deep regret that the committee bad allowed such an opportunity to slip. it wan unfortunate that one or two members of the Council seemed to have very great power over the others in matters of that kind. It was not the first time that a useful purchase had been frustrated. . . .

Councillor HENS)! ALL asked why it wen thlt the committee agreed to purchase property in Knotsford- road, of considerably less rental, at more than double the figure-that was fixed as the maximum for the Wilderspool property ? Either it was • joke or an attempt to block the whole thing. (Hear, hear). Such procedure made the Council look ridiculous. Councillor BELLIAN raid he was not ashamed of supporting the action of the committee. The maximum fixed woe twenty years' purchase on the assessment, and the majority of purchases by the Corporation in recent years had been made on that basis. It would he unwise to adopt such a high ligare as .050 as • precedent, for they would then have to pay proportionately for every piece of property they required in that neighbourhood. The committee bad before them a plan by which, if they could not acquire the property in question at • reasonable price, they could carry out an equally good scheme at. sawing of several thousand pounds to the Corporation. If anybody had an idea of purchasing property in order to get rich quick at the expense of the Corporation, he would find out his mistake.

Councillor PEMBERTON said the criticism which bad been piled on the heads of the committee was absurd because those who had spoken had no idea of tbe scheme contemptated by the committee. No scheme had teen accepted by the Council and he was not going to give the show away. Councillor ROBERTS : There is no show to give *WA y. Councillor PENT BE.RTON : That if a matter of opinion. There is too much known outside about the property which the Corporation requires. The people who shout the most are, in my opinion, the very people who gave tbta thing away. Alderman Emeriti:lt, I : Right you are. (Laughter.) Councillor RORER (to CO iinCillOr Pemberton) : You are the biggest shouter in this Council and out of it.

COIMCMOT VirLER : IS it correct that the pro- perty eas once offered privately to the Corporation for £400? . . .

The Tows CLERK No, it is not. Councillor BELLIAO: WILE it teas? The Tows CLERK Jib., never teen offored to the Corporation for an3thing like that Elan. It bas been contriderably more. The minutes were flies agreed to. " WHAT I HAVE SAID—"

The Sanitary Works Committee had called spun Mr. Councillor 'Ashford to withdraw certain remarks made at a meeting of the Town Council on the 3rd inst. with reference to tenders for begs. Councillor LASHFORD entered into deteila of the incident, contending that the committee bad confused two meetings, and said he considered his remora at the Council meeting meeting were justified. APer considerable discussion an amendment that the record be expunged from the minutes was brought forward by Councillor PENIBF.RTON who contended that Councillor Loshford bad cleared himself of the charge made by the committee. The amendment was defeated by 11 votes to three and the minutes were confirmed. COURCHIOT HAWTHORN said the incident en a storm in a teacup. NEW TOWN HALL KEEPERS.

It was resolved at a meeting of the Town Hall, Paris and Baths Committee, held on October 2nd, that Mr. G. W. Mitchell, of Liverpool, and his wife be appointed town hall keeper., at a joint glary of 35s per week, with rooms, coal, gas, Ste. The appointment was conOrmed. Councillor DICKINSON mentioned that there were 160 applications for the position.

div.head: OUR 'WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: OUR 'WATER SUPPLY.

Alderman JOHN EVANS reported that since the last meeting the Appleton reservoir, from which water for manufacturing purposes was supplied, had entirely failed. Advantage was taten of the opportunity to cleanse the reservoir, and that necessitated the destroy- ing of a large number of fish. With the mill- log assistance of the Warrioston Anglers' Asso- ciation, however, many fish were navel and transferred to the Bridgewater Canal. The transfer of Winwick water into the Appleton main had necessitated considerable extra pumping—in fact double the usual quantity was being pumped at Detail- lane. Since that heavy demand had been made, the well had been sinking at the rate of one inch per hoar— a very satisfactory result, proving that the supply at Wiowick was in excess of the requirements of the town for some time to come. (Hear. hear.) It was fortunate that the new main from Winsvick was completed ; otherwise the committee would bays Leon quite unable to core with the demand during the long drought.

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARY.
div.p: INCREASE OF SALARY.
The River Committee resolved that the salary of Mr. S. Jackson, river surveyor, be increased from £133 to £146 per annum as and from the Ist. prox., and this was agreed to.

COUNTY COUNCIL'S " IMPERTINENCE." A letter bad been received from the County Bridge, master taith reference to the supply of electric current for, and the working of, the proposed new Sankey Canal Bridge. The Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee resolve', " That this committee is not pre- pared to undertake the working of the bridge, but is willing to provide cables and current for the working of the bridge on payment by the County Council of the usual charges " Alderman SMETHUrtsr mid it would not be worth while spending the ratepayers' money in that way, especially when the County authorities had shown such little disposition to help the Corporation in bridge undertaking.. . . . .

Councillor Pia:BERTON Slid that if the County Council ezpected the Corporation to supply electrio current free of charge, it was a ridiculous proposition. Alderman J•MILS EVANS : But look what they are going to give us ! (Laughter). Councillor PAYBERTON said that considsring the yrs In which the County Council had treated Warrington, be did not know how they could have the impertinence to ask the Corporation to accede to their request. It was a pity there was not some Government department to which grown could appeal against a" tin pot com- mitttee " like that which dealt with the Lancashire roads. It was highly improper that, after the Corpora- tion had spent thousands of pounds on widening Liverpool-road, the County Council should be able to block their bridge scheme.

div.head: CONDITION OF THE ROADS.
div.p: THE CONDITION OF THE ROADS.

Councillor PEMBERTON called attention to the " deplorable" condition of thetramway track in Knots- ford-road. In some places it was positively dangerous. Alderman JAMES EVAN/ said Liverpool-road was equally dangerous—in fact the Corporation vnre endangering the houses of their own servants, as was shown by the accident to tbelFire Brigade on that road the other day. If the Corporation had to pay for all the damage that was done to vehicles through the bad condition of the roads, it would be a heavy bill to meet. Alderman Sortie error said people in charge of horses and vehicles would persist in keeping on the tramway track even when the road was a wide one. I,st year the committee paid over £Bto for repairing the roads and men were constantly employed in looking after them. The amount spent in the last two months was £lBO. If people thought they had cues against the Corporation, let them take them into Court and see what the Judge would say. Of course, if there was a Lad case the Corporation would try to settle it—(much lanchter)—lnit they would fight ony others. The minutes were approvtd.
MR. Roishar PIERPOINT. THE FREEDOM OF THE BOROUGH.

The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, which contained the following minute . "October 16th a meeting of the General Purposes Committee was held, when it was moved by the Mayor, seconded by Alderman Bolton, and unanimously resolved (I) That the Honorary Free- dom of the Borough be ccnferred upon Robert Pier. point, Req., J.P., for his eminent services rendered to the Borough ; (2) That a copy of the resolution con-1 (erring the freedom be suitably engrossed On vellum and presented in a casket to Mr. Pierpoint. His Worship said the resolution was an important one. Ile had never known any minute passed more cordially and unanimously. (Hear, bear.) Mr. l'ierpoint had repre- sented the town in Parliament for fourteen years and the Council thought that, on behalf of the people whom he had served, they should confer upon him a high honour. The DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded and said that in conferring the freedom upon Mr. Pierpoint they were doing honour to whom honour was doe.

Councillor HrtsnoLL: With regard to the casket, I presume an opportunity will be given to local trades- men to compete. The MAI on : Yes, they have all been invited. Alderman lieNtarr said the action of the Council in conferring the freedom upon Mr. Pierpoint would com- mend itself to every citizen of tbe town. Thee all bad the highest respect for Mr. Pierpoint as • Warring- tooian. For many years he had rendered signal services to the borough in the highest possible capacity. The Museum Committee had passed the following rerolution :—" That, in forwarding the usual letter of thanks for the donations recently received from Mr. Robert Pierpoinr. the committee desires to record its cordial appreciation of the many similar favours which the Museum has received from him during nemly 30 years, and to express the sincere regret of the members on Mr. Pierpoint's removal from the town." The resolution was cordially approved. THE BRIDGE.
RUMOURS OF DISAGREEMENT AND DELAY A CONTRADICTION.

On the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, Councillor CHANTLRR said it wruld be interesting to know the reser n for the recent delay in the erection of Warrington Bridge. The TowN CLRRK : There has been no delay. A rumour got about the town, but there is no foundation for it. DICKINSON IA it cot a fact that the men working on the bridge last Thursday were stopped from continuing their work by someone belonging to this place? The MAYOR : No, there is no truth in it. AlletMOß SMETH URST : The report WAS spread about but I, as chairman of the Bridges Committee, did not know anything about it, and so-one else seemed to know aiuthing either. I have been to the bridge this afternoon and the men are at work.

Councillor CIIANTLER : It is a fact that the men were stopped last week, through some disagreement. The Mk YOle : We ought to ask you the question if ' you know all about it and we don't. Councillor PEMBERTON said it was a pity if the work bad been stopped for two or three days. At any rate the Council might have been told about it. The work was going en so slowly that when there was a atoppage so soon after the commencement he did not blame the public for thinking that nothing was being done. Councillor CHANTLER There has been a disagree- ment, however much it may be kept beck. The MAYOR : My information is that there is no stoppage Councillor CHANTLER : It was with regard to the temporary footbridge. The Rev. E. C. E. CA RLEToN : That nytkes all the difference. __

Ihe PRIME MINISTER : The Corporation have to pot the buildings on. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON : That won't do. The PRIME MINISTER : I like to see the member for Truro come into this House, because we Snow what would happen if that typo of mind dominated the government of this country. We should have to prey very passionately' God help old England." Continuing the Frime Minister submitted quotations to show that several of the "alleged " leaders p f the Tory party, including Mr. Balfour, accepted the principle of the taxation of land values. The Rev, E. C. E. CARLETON : I did not touch land values.

The I'aistc MINISTER : I don't like to suggest that the hon. member does not know the meaning of words. Some 600 rating authorities, promeded the Prime Minister, had expressed themselves in favour of the adoption of the principle. 'I he taxation of land values had been discussed at least twice in a Tory House of Commons and a Bill had even been carried in that assembly. Under tbe present land system every facility was given to landlords to withhold land from use and to impose a tariff on industry and labour, worse than any tariff which the foreigner could raise against them. He defied the member for Truro to point out that the State recognized real ownership in land, even at the present time. Ile contended that the values which the people bad created should be taxed for the benefit, of the community. The present system of locking up the land involved a deduction from the wages that ought to be paid to labour and absorbed benefits which should go to relieve the lot of the people and improve the standard of Hying. Mr. E. OSBORNE (I.' Newcastle•on•Tyne) said the Prime Minister had spoken As if the whole Hill could be summed up in the taxation of land values, but it embodied a great deal more. One important provision was that which forbade the allocation of prcffts from municipal undertakings to the relief of rates. How would that apply to Doncaster and Cheater, where the rates were considerably redacted by the profits derived from race course*? Did Ha Government propose to give the people racing for nothing ? (Leughter.) Some municipalities held licensed property. Was is suggested that they should cheapen the liquor or let the tenant have the house rent free? If all the pron.' from the markets in Warrington were to be returned to the stall- holders, what about the competition, which was already great,with the shopkeepers who paid rates ?He contended that if the Corporation could make a profit out of Cs markets it should certainly do no and apply it to the relief of rates. With regard to the trarnwa)s, it was unfair that the ratepayers who bad had to pay for their construction should be ignored when it came to a question of profits. Ile consilered that a bigger fraud had never been imposed on the House than the methods to be adopted for the valuation of land and buildings. The taxation of land valuer, which they would like to see in operation, MEI not touched properly in the Bill. The Chancellor of the Exchequer had inveighed against the brewing interest, but the only tax he proposed for " the trade" was to be levied on the licence-bolder. The brewer could do what be like and no tax would be inflicted on him. However, they miglt he sure that when the Chancellor talked of relieving "the trade" of £20,060,000 of taxation with one hand, he intended to take £10,000,000 from them with the other.(Laughter and applause.) The Bill had been badly drafted, it would never operate suzceasfully, and the time of the House might have been devoted to something mire useful. The LEADER or 'THE OPPOSI nom (Mr. W. H. Stans- field) said the vehemence of the Prime Minister's remarks showed that the capable speech of the member for Truro must have gone home. This country must be governed by all types of mind and the Prime Minister's prayer might very well be offered for BOMB members of his own party who made smells of the government. The Prime Minister contended that the landowners did nothing for the land, but the fact was self evident that if any class did their duty, the landlords were doing theirs towards the land. Because one landowner bare and there might be defective, it came with bad grace !from Radicals to rail at the whole clam. Some of the points in the Bill, he admitted, were good. He was not, however, in favour of the profits from the trams being devoted to the reduction of the fares. Warriostoniana who lived on the tram routes suffered great annoyance from the noise, and it would be unfair for outsiders, who travelled to and from the town on the cars, to have the benefit of the profits. If the Chancellor believed that 90 per cent, of the poverty and crime of the country was due to drink, why did he propose to saddle" the trade "with caly 75 per cent. of the cost ? If we had a reasonable system of tariffs, poverty would be considerable diminished. (Laughter and epplause.) Why did not the Chancellor go the whole hog and levy a Inc on skating rinks, football matches (et which betting often took place), and music halls, which were responsible for a certain amount of crime and poverty ? The CH AN( ELLOR OF TIT E EXCHEQUER (Mr. J. Jarman) in replying to the discussion, raid the freeholder was in no sense bit by the Bill. Ile would be butter off because the rating of other people's land would tend to the reduction of his rates. It was absolutely untrue to suggest that the Govern- ment selected several classes of the community for punishment under the Bill. Apparently the only law which the me-obey for Truro recognised was Tory- made law. (Laughter.) Land could be and was valued apart frdm the buildings in Warrington. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON : Give me one case.

The CH ANCELLOR OF THE ECG II F 41.7 ER The Co-operative Society's central premises in Sankey- street. With regard to the taxation of the" trade," the Lulk of the houses were owned by the brewers so it would not be the publican but the man who manufac- tured the beer who would bare to pay. The Opposition amendment that the Bill he read six months hence was defeated and the measure was agreed to without a division.

They had, he said, not only been pleased but delighted at Dr. Joseph's occupancy of the chair. On behalf of some of the rowdy or noisy members—(laughter)—he wished to say that if at any time they caused his Worship any trolible they aincerely regretted it. Everything that could be done by a mayor had been done by Dr. Joseph, and in such • manner as to add to the dignity of the office and the well-being of the town. (Applause). Alderman Ditxurrr, in seconding, remarked that his I Worship had made an ideal Mayor, both in his conduct I of municipal affairs and the readution with which he bad thrown himself into every good work in the town. Alderman FORSIIANN, in identifying himself with the motion, expressed pleasure that Dr. Joseph was goiag to be the Mayor for another twelve months. He associated with the proposition the name of Hiss Joseph. for the admirable and graceful way In which she hod carried out the duties of 'Mayoress. . .

Alderman SNIFTRURST also eulogised the services of the Slayer end Mayoress during the pest twelve months. Councillor PEMBERTON said the Mayor had discharged his duties with dignity, courtesy, justice and forbear- ance. (Hear, hear.) Aiderran JAMES EVANS said be hoped the Council would from that night make a point of strictly obey- ing the chair. Aldermen PIER MINT said he could give an absolute promise to be as quiet as a mouse during the next twelve months. (Laughter). The motion was further supported by Councillors Hawthorn, Toole, Locker, Archer, Creik, Jenkins, Wilkinson and Skelland,aud was heartily carried. The MAYOR., who was received with applause, raid he had conscientiously tried to fulfil the promise he made upon his election. Candidly speaking, he did not think he could have done more than he had tried to do. (Applause.) The past year had been en important and historic one. It began with the general election and other events had included the great colliery disaster (Warrington contributing £SOO to the relief fund), the Coronation celebrations, which entailed a great deal of work and anxiety, and the inauguration of the bridge scheme. He did not think any members of the Council, except thorn who had occupied the chair, knew tbe large amount of social work in which the Mayor had to take part. Ile would like to know, as a matter of curiosity, bow many meetings he bad attended and how many epeeches he had made. In thanking the Council for their unvarying kindness and courtesy, the Mayor said be thought nothing of occasional ebullitions of excite- ment such as were bound to happen in a body of men who were fighting for one goc d aim—the good of the town they represented. He respected them all the more for it, especially when they afterwards expressed regret that anything untoward should have occurred. The Mayor concluded with an exprension of thanks to the permanent officials for their kind aesistauce.

div.head: rOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: rOCAL PARLIAMENT.
REV. I C. E. CARLETON'S CHALLENGE CAUSES A BREEZE.
Rating Bill Passed.

There were some lively passages in the adjourned debate on the Bill for the readjustment of local rating, at the meeting of the Warrington Parlismentary Debating Society on Tuesday evening. The Deputy Speaker (Mr. .1. MoDermid) presided over a good attendance. . .

Mr. PETER DAVEN,'ORT (C, West Salford) said the Conservatives viould be open to the charge of derelic- tion of duty If they did not oppose to the utmost proposals so unfair and vindictive as were contained in the Bill. If the Liberals thought they could cheapen land by taxing it they must for ever abandon their principal argument in, favour of Free Trade. (Laughter and applaute.) The lend taxes would be unjust to a very respectable end law abiding section of the community—be did not mean the big landlords and dukes, but the email freeholders. This Bill made no exceptions in favour of agricultural land, and the farmer would thervfore be hit by it. It was not every landowner who had the means of developing bin land, and he contended that land which bore no income should not be taaed, but should be treated in the same way as an untenanted house. It should be their endeavour to improve the housing of the people, but the Bill would have the effect of diminehing the land space allotted to each house, and would therefore place more difficulties in the path of the social reformer. _ _

The PREfIDET OF THE BOARD OF TRADE (Nfr. M Howarth) said the Member for St. Alban's (NIL E. A White) had suggested that if the rating of small die-. Dicta were left In the hands of Parish Councils, large owners of land and property might resort to some j subterfuge to get rid of their ust burden. Evidently he had a worse opinion of the landlord class than the Liberals had. (Laughter.) The greatest objection which the Conservatives had urged against the Bill was the hardship to small owners which they contended might accrue if the land clauses were retrospective. Perhaps there might be such a grievance in one out of 10,000 cases, and the Government would find means in the Budget or by other legislation of removing it. The small freeholders were not the gentlemen they were trying to get at. The clauses were aimed at the great Is odlords who had accumulated wealth by the industry of others. (Applause). The Government intended to make them pay, (Applause). The taxes on liquor were not intended as a temperance measure, but it was a wise arrangement that part of the profit cn the sales of drink should be devoted to the expenditure on poverty and crime which were largely produced by the traffic. The only regret he had was that the clause would probably reduce the price of r rink. He believed that the dearer they could make drink the less they would sell. He congratulated the Conservatives en the intellectual progress they had made on social questions since they had shaken themselves free from Tariff Reform. (Laughter). It was a significant thing that the Bill had not been dubbed 4` Socialism " but some of its principles bad actually been claimed as Conservative. (Laughter and applause). The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON (C., Truro) said the great question they hod to consider was: were the propossls of the Bill honest and in accordance with the principles , of justice? The Prime Minister had told the Unioniats , that while they were anxious to have Dreadnoughts they objected to the taxation that was necessary to pay for them. That was en inaccurate statement. The Unionists were quite willing to pay but they objected to a method of taxation which introduced the principle of favouritism and unfairness into the region of revenue. The method of the Radical Government was to pick out at their discretion certain people, classes, interests and ineustries, upon whom the hulk of the financial burden was to be laid in order that it might le made lighter for other people. Consequently the levies thus made were sot taxes but fines and penalties, and the people upon whom they were laid were treated as felons. People who had broken no law and were guilty of no crime were selected for punishment. Parliament thus invaded the jurisdiction of the Courts and the King's ' subjects stood to lose portions of their property; at any moment, on the sentence of a Minister, without being allowed that fair trial which wan the inalienable right of every Engliehman. Many of the Liberal party apparently did not Snow what English rights were. (Laughter). The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHWteER ITe knew what wrongs are. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, 'continning, acid the authors of the Bill were so anxious to fine and injure the landlord that they did not care how it was done. At a recent meeting of the Land Union he gave a challenge to the, fleck that it was not possible to value land apart from any house's or buildiegs that were erected thereon. The method of Mr. Lloyd George as indicated in Form IV., did not give the true value. lie (the speaker) suggestrd that Market Gate should be taken as a centre and circle described, having a radius of a quarter of a mile. They could take ane shop or house within that area and he would undertal I, to show that the value of the land could not be ascertained apart from the buildings, according to Mr. Lloyd George's method. When the Warrington Corporation had to acquire property for the purpose of widening Bridge-street, the building, were included in the valua- tion, as • matter of course. Mr. Lloyd George had been trying to invent a value of his own, but the only true value was the moiling value. . _ .

The PRIMP. Mititsvan (Mr. E. Wynne Jones) said he hoped that next time the member for Truro came to the House he would be able to discuss the Bill before the H 00543 and not a Budget passad by a previous Government.
_ The Rev. E. C. E. CsnurroN : The principles ere aII in this Bill.

The PRIME MINISTER: The underlying principle of the Bill is taxation of land for rating purposes. The Member for Truro says there lea difficulty in valuing land apart from the buildings. Thera is not the sliahteet difficulty in doing anything of the kind. The Rev. B.C. E. CARLETON : Will you sect pt my challeoge ? The PRIME MINISTER : I. accept your challenge. (Applause.) It is hardly fair to interfere with the time allowed me in the debate, but on any future occasion the member for Truro likes to In I should be glad to accept the challenge he bas thrown out to-night. Ile eats you cannot value land apart from the property. The landlord who wanted to sell laud to the Corpora- tion for a school in Lovely-lane knew the value of that land.

div.head: TERRITORIAL ARMY AMENDMENT BILL, 1911.
div.p: THE TERRITORIAL ARMY AMENDMENT BILL, 1911.
Nt Tuetday evening the Territorial Army Amend- ment Bill, 11, will be introduced by the Secretary for War (Captain H. Cl. Roberts). Its provisiots are as follows

_ 1. lhere shall be added to the present establishment of 14 divisions 3 diviskos which shall be recruited in Ireland. They shall be governed by County Associa- tions having bend quarters in Dublin, Cork and London- derry, and shall be IMOREI respectively as the Eastern, Southern and North-Western divisions. _ .
2. Each division shall be commanded by • regular general ollic4r and elch brigadv shall be commanded by a regular ofkaer no below the rank of calonel. "' ' "

a , - 31e regulations relating to the liability of mem- bers of the Force shall be altered as follows: (a) that all combatant I Ulcers shall be required to attend a class of instruction at Ilythe for Musketry, and also to attend School " or be attached to a Regular Depot for that branch of the service to which they belong for the full period laid down in Army Regulations. Both these requirements must be condi- tional upon officers obtaining the •• puttlt " allowance and must be completed within two years of joining. (b) Recruits of all ranks shall be required to put in at least 60 drills during their first year of which 30 most be recorded before attending the annual training. All trained won must put in 40 drills instead of 10 as now.
(c) That all ranks when attending the knout' training shall be required to attend for the fall period of 15 days and that separation allowancOggill be paid to all N C.O.'s and men.

(d) That all men shall be paid for attending drills at the rats of two drills minal one days' army pay with- out allowance.. Each drill shall consist of at least One hour's training and all drills of longer duration than three boors shall be paid for am one day's pay. The payment for attendance at drills shall only ripply to drills after the first 20 have been recorded by trained men. and 30 by recruits. 4 The permanent staff, i.e. the adjutant, sergeant major, and sergeant instructors, to the number of one per company, shall be appointed to each Tertitorial , unit. An adjutant who,by his seal and g I military ability raises the discipline, moral, and generally thel tone of the condition of the otit. to which he is attached, shall receive recognition by the payment of a bonus on the expiration of Isis appointment, and a report from the G.O.C. shall be sent to the C.O. of the battalion the es-adjutant rejoins in the form of • confidential report.

5 The bonus shall he a sum nut exceeding and shall only be paid on the recommendation of the General Officer commanding the division. 6 That rifle rangen shall he provided within reancn- able distance of the headquarters of every Infantry Regiment. -
7 That permanent nummer camps be ornanized where men can fire and drill, on full pay, on Saturday. and Sundays at least one of the. week-nod ramps to be undertaken before the annual training.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Percy Howl and et mpany enjoy an enviable reputation in the music ball world and, therefore, one can understand the huge crowds which bane attended the Palace and Hippodrome this week. The premier performance is not of a stereotyped nature by any means, and it fully warrants the title of a new musical phantasy. It is unique in every way and the acting is aptly blended with the strains of various musical instruments. There are no less than tight scenes— it is obvious that the production is on a large scale—and the one which appeals to us in greatest measure is that of the Demon Wood. this scene is brilliant and artistic and Mr. Honri as the Demon scores a great success. The band and the orchestra are a treat in themselves, palpaltly evincing the true musical talent. As a comedian Charles Lee is popular with all sections of the house, his eccen- tricities and his stories being decidedly original. The Oxford Boys 'give a skilful exhibition of harmonic dancing and also contribute some pleasing songs. A. pretty seems entitled " The Cingalee " is presented by , the Sisters Cora, who have previously entertained I Warrington audiences. Phil and Nettie Peters are exemplary German-American ccinedy entertainers and home Resaire is a fascinating soubtett dancer. The pictures are exceptionally good.

div.head: LAUNDRESS'S ' SIMPLE ' INJURY.
div.p: A LAUNDRESS'S ' SIMPLE ' INJURY.
29 Years' Torture from Poisoned Legs.
ZASI-81.-K CURE • HELPLESS CRIPPLE.

A simple injury, aggravated by the foolish use of • " cheap' ointment, so crippled Mn. C. Brown that she had to give up • profitable laundry " Nhile hanging out clothes twenty yearn ago," Mrs. Brown, who lives at 17, Exeter Terrace, Salisbury, told a reporter, "I slipped from • stool and knocked my left leg against the edge of a metal bucket. The skin was torn away, leaving a long nasty wound which wouldn't heal. Later the whole limb became inflamed and swollen, and a discharge ran from the wound. I very foolishly tried a home- made preparation, which set up fermentation. Sores b-ohs tot all over the limb, and as a result of putting all my weight on my right leg, that became ulcerated as well. Both legs wore black with disease, and skin and flesh seemed quite rotten. " I had finally to give up my laundry, as I could , scarcely more about. I was often in such awful , agony that I bit my pillow and screamed out. If it hadn't been for the kindness of friends I really don't know what we should have done, for I was positirelyi helpless. Then I was an inmate of the Salisbury ' Infirmary, and afterwards had treatment at the Southampton Hospital. At both institutions I received every attention, but my legs simply wouldn't heal. For many months I paid fortnightly visits to a Southampton specialist, and then gave up, thoroughly disheartened. I took to ony bed, too weak to even look after myself. " A neighbour at last persuaded me to try Zorn- Buk, and she was kind enough to come in every day and dress my legs with the balm, after washing them with Zara-Buk Medicinal Soap. I cant describe the relief Zamlledt yore me ! I had known nothing like it for nearly 20 years. Careful perseverance with Zam-Buk showed me that it was actually healing my legs. The great sores stopped throbbing and running, and began to clone up, after discharging all corrup- tion. Beth legs healed up, and erer every Bose Zone- Thaicgreu. new skin, until there wasn't a bit of dinease about either limb."

div.head: NOTES BY " OVALIST."
div.p: NOTES BY " OVALIST."

As expected, Warrington's concern in the destina- tion of the Lancashire Cup has soon come to an end. They played a capital game at Widnes, but fortune was against them, and the home side won by ¶1 points to 5 points. S. far as the play went,the teams were OD level terms, and the game confirmed my view that Warrington wou'd give the Widnesians a better match than they did laet seasco.

There was a time in Satutday's game when the Wirepullera looked like turning the tables on Widnes. The latter were only leading t1..5 and Warrington were attacking vigorously, when Ike Taylor sustained an injury to his knee which was no severe that he had to be taken aw.ty in the ambulance. Thualhandicappel. Warrington's chance was gone, but they made a plucky struggle to the end. Widnes got three tries in the game. but two of them were of a lucky character, and I have little doubt that the Wirepullers will put ptil to the Widnes account when the teams meet at Wilderspool.

Chief honours on the Warrington side go to the forwards, who played a great game, and fairly got the better of the Widnes six. Thomas and Arnold played a brilliant game, and the form of the Welsh- man just now entitles him to be considered far repre- sentative matches. Woodburn was a failure in the centre, and will need to reproduce some of his form in the opening match of the season to gain favour again with the Warrington crowd. He and Bradshaw hanged placze at half-iiine, and Bradshaw was such a success in the middle that he is retained there to-day. Even Tilley had an off-day on Saturday, and was slow in getting to the ball—and to the man with it, when Reid scored. Waysvell's try was a beauty, and viggests that he is fast coming back into form.

At a meeting of the Lancashire C-mnty Committee at Manchester on Monday night, the draw for the aecond round of the Lancashire Senior Cup, to be played on November 24th, resulted : Wigan v. St. Helens Widnes v. Coventry Broughton Rangers v. Rochdale Htrnets Oldham v. Leigh

I learn that Taylor's injury turns out to be less serious than was at first feared, though it will he Boma weeks before he can think of playing again. We :ould do with the plucky and reli4ble Widnesian when the Colon'ala visit Wilderspool on Deeeraher 30th.

Warrington resume League football again to-day Ind should make further progress in the League at the expense of Rochdale Hornets. 'the latter hardly seem as strong as they were a season ago, when they were only two points behind the Warrington score of 18 prints, but a great deal will depend on the home forwards with such stalwarts as Taylor and Brooks absent. The latter has got a strained thigh and had to decline an invitation to play against the Australians it Everton. He will be all right in another week.

div.head: FRAWLEY ON THE TRANSFER.
div.p: FRAWLEY ON THE TRANSFER.

- I learn that the Wartington Club have at last decided to put Frawley on the transfer list at 1,150. This is no fancy figure, but what they expect to get. He should be worth that to the Colonials, and to more than one League Club. What offers from Oldham and Hull ? The Warrington attitude seems to be that as Frawley will not play for Warrington, they had better realise on him. It derends a good deal on where he goes as to what the Wsrringt in crowd will have to say.
--- Mr. Osborne of the Warrington Committee had an interesting column in the " Athletic News "on Mon- day, in which he discussed very fully the Frawley case. I quote the following :

div.head: FORM AND THE RYLANTs.
div.p: THE FORM AND THE RYLANTs.

As a member of the committee of the Warrington 'RC., writing with the full feels of the case before ma, and in an individual capacity,! shall state the matter fairly, and endeavour to remove some of the charges. At the outset, I hardly need emphasise the fact that the club has always treated Frawley fairly—that has never been disputed by him. What he has slid, however. Is that he thought when he' signed on 'be was binding himself to the clab for one season only. If any such doubt has arisen in his mind, it is not attributable to the executive, but may have been caused, perhaps, by the form which is used by the Union for the purposes of registering a profes- sional player. I must confess that Form "A" is somewhat mis- leading, and that the professional rules are vague. All professionals are registered on this form, end the registration is binding for only one season. It is only when we come to the Northern League by-laws, that the omission is remedied, and Rules 18,17, and 18 are explicit enough. But the form referred to is the only form (apart from the agreement), and in practice it has worked successfully. Hitherto it hen never been challenged. Every player knows when he is placed on a club's register that before he can play for another club be most get his transfer.

RATIYIND BY NEW SOUTH WALES. The point at issue then, no for as Frawley Is con- cerned, is not no much that he does not want to play for Warrington—as a matter of fact he has told me that he does—but be thinks thst he is entitled tn another "lump sum." Having, as be says," signed on " to play for one season only, he believes himself to be

free to negotiate again for the i.e of his services. Such a position is untenable. With the exception of Sidney Dean, who, I sin pleated to tee, has since decided to play again for his old club, Frawley is the only player who bee com- plained of the " drastic resolution." In fact, I doubt very much whether either of them ever considered the resolution in that light at all. But .that does not matter. If the resolution was no had as it is made out to be, why has it been ratified by the N.S.W. League ?

M 1.-TP AL RESPECT REte I RED. But if Frawley has on agreement with Use represen- tative* of the New South Wales Lengueas is stated,thst opens out a wider issue. Either the agreement was made owing to a misunderstanding, or t`_ay are challenging the ruling of the Northern." Union Committee. If the former, it is to be regretted- I fail to see, however, how they have been misled ; for tin generally boo on that the League knew full well that be was a registered player of Warrington and they were informed that he could not play either in Australia or here without Warrington'. consent. They persisted in allowing him to play there, notwith- standing the pronouncement of the Northern Union Committee, and, taking upon themselves a self- imposed authority, they insist upon sending him over to play with the touring team, flaring broken the agreement once, they think they can do an again. There is much talk of all the C.lonials now signed on with the various Northern Lillian clubs leaving in a body at the end of the season on a worm's tour. When they have departed we shall probably devote more of our time and money in " teachine the young endeavour how to shoot "—or, rather, bow to score tries. The time is now ripe. If that end is accomplished some of us, at any rate, will not think that the " fiasco" hal been altogether in vain.

div.head: LANCASHIRE CUP.
div.p: LANCASHIRE CUP.
Warrington's 111-Luck at Widnes.

The first round of the Lancashire Cup on Saturday drew Warrington and Widnes together at Widnes. There was a lot of rain in the morning, but just before the match started the weather cleared, and there was a capital crowd of 5,000. Warrington bad a somewhat experimental side, for in addition to the re-shueliag of the three-quarter line, Brooks was unable to appear, and Daintath filled the vacancy. Teams: Widnee—Jones, back ; Seinton, Laws, Lally, and Reid, three-quarter backs; Noon and O'Gara, half ' backs; S Assay, G Aspey, Lloyd, Johnson, Rigby and M'Cartby, forwards. Warrington—Tilley, back ; Bradshaw, Taylor, Wood- bare, and Waywell, three-quarter backs ; Creevey and Daintitb, half-backs ; Johnson, Arnold, Thomas, Cheaters, Brocklehurst and Shugars, forwards. Referee, Mr F Renton, Hunslet. Touch judges, Messrs Johnson, Rochdale and Foulkes, St. Helens. Play °reined in lively fashion and it was early to be seen that Warrington were going to make a fight of it. , The forwards were very energetic, and useful work by ' the halves and Bradshaw resulted in an attack in the Widnes quarter. Thomas, Johnston, Arnold and Brocklehurat mode dashing raid, and Lally was lucky to save the situation. Laws and Swinton drove the Wirepullera out again and this time the invasion bad substantial reward for after Lally, O'Gara and Reid bad handled the sphere, the Warrington goal was severely menaced. Loose play placed Woodburn in possession, but he failed to hold the ball when tackled, and Reid, had the simplest of tries. The appeal of the visitors against the legitimacy of the point wag ignored. Jones , missed the goal kick. Following on a raid of the Warrington goal by Lally and the Bro:hers Aspey on resuming, the" Wirepuller!'" exhibited splendid dash in another raid, and the home team being toe premature were penalized, and Thomas coolly dropped a goal from near the half-way line. Both aides enteredento the play with rare energy and Shugare and Thomas came in for notice when they dribbled along the reserve touch and Swinton WAS decidedly lucky in saving the sitation when he played the ball into touch. Near the interval Reid was placed in possession on the right, and this time he eluded Waywell and Tilley making a week tackle, Reid scored the second try. Jones again missed the goal-kick. Halftime was reached without any addition to the score. Widnes, two ! tries (sic points), Warrington one goal (two points). ! Changing ends it was seen that the Warrington three- quarter Hoe was re-arranged, Woodburn and Bradshaw ! on the right wing having exchanged places. The ! " Wirepuliers "were very aggressive, the forwards in particular introducing any amount of vim into their rushing tactics. Themis was almost over lifter a fine ! effort, superior numbers accounting for him. Creevey breaking away from a pack made considerable progress until he handed the ball to Waywell. The latter dodged Reid and after • brilliant run scarred the try of the match. Thomas failed at goal. Warrington again made headway and the Chemicals had certainly an anxious time of it. Taylor made a particularly Use effort to get through but was badly hurt in the tackle. Ile was eventually carried away on the ambulance. This ruined Warringtonle chances, though from • cross kick Woodburn had a clear field, but to tbe consternation of the visiting enthusiasts he failed. S. Aspey scored for Widnes in a forward rush. Final : Widnes 3 tries (9 points). Warrington I goal, I try, (5 point sl. RUNCORN WELL-BEATEN AT BROUGHTON.

Played at Broughton,the attendance numbering abou 8,000. When the game had been in progress seven minutes Richardson opened the score for Runcorn with a goal from a mark. The Rangers still pressed, and their efforts were at length rewarded with a try by Winskill, who scored after a bad mull. The place-kick failed, but a few minutes later Davidson placed a goal from a penalty kick. At the interval the Rangers led by 1 goat I try (5 points) to I goal (2 points). The second half opened very evesly, the game being mostly confined to the forwards. It was not long before the Rangers increased their lead. div.head: LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
Conversazione.

In connection with the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, a conversazione was held in the Town Hall on Monday evening, and was attended by over 250 members and their lady friends at the invita- tion of Mr. W. Si!cook, the president Mr. OSWALD LOFTHOCSE (hon. secretary), said it was a pity that • county borough with a population of nearly 80,000 should have a Literary and Philosophical Society with only 150 members. (Hear, hear). He hoped that at the next meeting he would have a long list of new members to announce. (Hear, hear and applause). Mr. Sil.ooclC mid it was thought that the opening meeting should take the form of a conversazione, such as that which was being held, as it might be the means of bringing the members together and infusing greater interest In the work of the society. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The programme of tl e evening was exceedingly en)oyable, a floe Beleztion of artiste being chosen. Sties E. Taylor contributed Elgars song (• The Swimmer," which she rendered in her usually skilful style. During the evening she also sang " Softly awakes my heart," "How many • lonely caravan," and "My mother bids me bind my hair." Distinctly popular items were the pianoforte solos of Miss Clare Newell. With the ability ehich this young lady has alwsys charmed audiences she played "Prelude" (Mendelasohn) " Rhapsody " (Liszt) and " Caprice " (Gluck-Saint Seem). Miss Adams sweetly sang " Birds in the High Hall "and "Oh that we two were Maying "and as an encore" liala Liebe Dick " (Grieg). Musical recita- tions entitled" Bait " and " Plinustones " were ably given by Miss Dorothy Browne, and a sketch entitled " The Superfluous Hat "(Sirs. Barry Pain) t Misses Adams, Browne and Lofthouse, showed forth to advant- age their capable histrionic abilitie• During the evening refreshment, were served, the catering being in the hands of Mies Ashurst, Bridge- street.

A vote of thanks was accorded to the MAYOR (Coun- cillor Dr. Joaeph) for allowing the society the use of the Council Chamber and the proceedings terminated with a similar compliment to the artistes on the proposition of Mr. Silcock seconded by the Rev. 11. V. IPigot.

div.p: October 28, 1911
WARRINGTON WORKS BOWLING ASSOCIATION.
Individual Merit Competition.
A CLOSE FINISH.

The closing stages of the annual handicap of the Individual Merit Competition of the Warrington Bowling Association were witnessed on Saturday at the headquarters the Horse and Jockey Inn, by a large gathering of bowling enthusiasts. The 'acmes which ban attended this main is remarkable, no fewer than 50 works entering with a total of 483 players, and taking eight Saturday afternoons to complete the games. Some excellent bowling has been I ema right through the competition, hut especially in the closing stages, while in the final. which was fought in the serni-darknets, the result hung in the balance right to the close. Tbe finalists, 1: Jackson, of Croatleldt, and W Langley, of Rylandv, are to be complimented on their grand aisplay, the former mutually r noing oat victors by 15 points to 12. At the clone of the match, Captain Croafleld, the ptealdent of the Association, presented the cup to the

successful competitor. The President was also supported by Alderman Forshaw, Messrs W Webster and C Leigh (vice-presidents), J Rillett (chairman of the Committee), G liall (vice-chairman), J A Rush- worth (treasurer) and W Patrick (secrwary). Mr. WILLETT said he thought he would be voicing the thoughts of all present that afternoon when he said that they had in their president (Captain Croatleld) the right man in the right place. (Hear, hear.) Since Captain Crostield had taken over that position, some- thing like nine years ago, the nesociation had pro- gressed by leaps and bounds until they had that year " broken the record ' by having an entry of 30 work. I with a membership of 483 players. (Applause.) That had only been achieved by the tact of their having such a worthy president at their head. Captain CROSFIELD said he bad immensely enjoyed the games that afternoon and he was glad to see that the men had played like true eportcner. He was delighted that they bad had each a grand entry, the number comparing very favourably with the total for the previous year. Mr. T. JACKSON, the cup winner, in reply to repeated calls for" epeech,” said that since his entry into the competition he had improved by sixteen every year, Until 03ve he had succeeded in gaining the coveted trophy.

div.head: TOWN BEAUTIFUL.
div.p: THE TOWN BEAUTIFUL.
WARRINGTON'S STANDING.

The second of (be three illustrated lectures entitled "Town Planning in Prutice " use delivered by Mr. Henry R. Aldrich° in the Parr Halton Tuesday evening. There was again a sparse but representative attendance, presided over by Mr. C. E Parker. The CHAIRVAN said there never was a time in the history of this country when more earnest thought was given to the social conditions under which we lived Never in the history of this borough had no much intelligent and sympathetic thought been given to those things which hots directly upon the health and general well-being of those who reside in this town. And it was fitting that this thought and action should be end was being directed along civil lines. The particular phase of the subjtct for that evening woe" Town Planning in its relation to Public Health and Municipal Economy." To his mind, it Mr. Aldridge could prove that Town Planning conduced to ;moll° health he would have made good his cue for Municipal Economy. Apart altogether from the important considera- tions which might arise in connection with inch questions as the economy in road making and it Town Planning conduced to public, health the charges in poor rate, Sm., became lighter end the result W3B municipal , economy. Not only no, but if through better housing ' conditions the vitality of town dwe'lers had increased all round the ability of those who had to hear the burden of the rates was necersarily increased. We must all recognise the truth of whet hi• wotship the Mayor said about. the disastrous legacy we bad inherited from our forefathers in connection with town building. Through the mistakes, the negligence, and the ignor- ance of the pest, we were inheritors of had conditions. and it would takes long time, and he a dificult teak to undo the mistakes of the past. But he believed that amongst the people of this borough, emorgat the leading citizens, amongst those who ungradgingly gave their time and energy in our Town Council, there was a willingness to adopt any well thought out practical scheme for the improvement of cur town. They had to acknowledge that while the condi- tions of the houses in which the pooter section of our people lived might not be worse than the average of industrial towns in this country, still they had to confess that that average was a very low one. To mans the ideaconveyed in the term of "The Homes of Merry England " was an echo of a far off ege, and conveys little meaning to them.
HOME SHOULD BE THE ENGLISHMAN. 9 CASTLE

the place around which his beet life interests should gather, it was the keystone of the nation. It ought to be the credle of an imperial race. A nation's wealth was not in its possessions. or its gold,but in its men, women, and children,—stalwart, vital, sober, and virtuous. Such could not be raised in slume. Shame upon us if we allowed to continue the effect of bad laws, indifference and ignorance. We must break ills entail of our past. (Applause.) What could we expect from the environment we have allowed to gather around Use homes of the poor' The homelessness of the masses was not a mere figure of speech, it was an ugly naked truth, • deep seated canker, destroying the nation's vitality. What interest in national life, what interest in municipal life, what stake in the country, had a slim dweller? We must give him some visible spot, some decent home and surroundines, to shich his humanity could cling, and horn whith his citizenship, and his patriotism,could take their rise.We boasted that we were citizens of an Empire upon which the son never set but what matters this to the man and woman upon whose back yard the sun never rose. (Applause.) The greatest danger of this country was not the social unrest which might take forms which some might conaider dangerous as well as Utopian. A far greater danger arose from the imperfect undeveloped lines of those who were indifferent to their own, on well as their country's wellbeing, the men who lived merely animal lives, who neither raw the visions or dreamed the dreams of ores. It might sometimes be their faults, hut more often it was the hint of their surroundings Be it ours to see to it that such had a fair chance by the creation of • healthy environment. (Applause.) Mr ALDRIDGE, who received a cordial welentro raid that practically without exception the most beautifel cities in the world owed a large part of their beauty to foresight and care in town planning mad the duty of town planning only needed to be recognised to be faithfully fulfilled. The overwhelming weight of authority of the past was not, however, sufficient for • modern community, and it was absolutely [KAU., to demonstrate the case for town planning in regard to modern needs. What he does contribute is a temperament. If he is not deep, he is at least original, and there is something more than that in his character. He never appears to surprise others so much as he surprises him- self. He begins to address the House with, as it would appear, no particular intention,' and then an idea strikes him, and he becomes delightful. It was only a second thought which led him on Monday to speak of the laboriousness of Parliamentary life and the heavy tasks that were laid, not only on Ministers, but on ordinary members. Then his mind opened out in a manner that we suppose must have been surprising tc him- self. Probably it never came across his thoughts that he was the author of the system in which he found so much to condemn.

The Board of Trade has UNEMPLOYMENT IN j ust published an SEPTEMBER. exhaustive Report on the Labour market, in the current number of the "Labour Gazette." It shows that the percentage of unemploy- ment last month was 29 per cent—a lower percentage of unemployment than in any corresponding month of the past ten years. On the other hand, the reports from foreign countries show practi- cally no improvement as compared with 1910. The Trade Union Reports in France actually show a higher percentage of unemployment than in 1910. The industries of this country have not, as yet, experienced any serious set-back as a result of labour unrest. As a matter of fact, the volume of trade has been steadily increasing, as is shown by the con- tinued improvement in railway traffic returns as compared with 1910.
At a time when we are THE COTTON TRADE. rejoicing at the brisk —A CONTRAST. state -of our cotton . .

--- trade,despite the doleful predictions of the Tariff Reformers, it is interesting to see the contrast with the cotton trade in Germany. Press reports of last week-end show that the situation in the German Cotton Industry has grown even worse than it was several months ago. One important mill at Munchen Gladbach has suspended with-liabilities of about £200,000, and another suspension of less importance has occurred. Among the mills it is said that this has been the worst year that they have had since the position of the trade began to grow worse several years ago. Weaving mills are also complaining of bad business conditions ; their summer orders from the home market scarcely reached half of their usual volume. And yet, according to the rariff Reformers, Germany was knocking us out, and we were told that our only chance was to adopt the system of Protection, which was enabling them to do it !

Sir JOHN FALSTAFF was • less delighted because he was a wit in himself than on the ground that he was the cause that laughter was in others. That is just Mr. BALFOUR'S case. He seems to be surprised at his own happiness in producing a cheerful and even laughing temper in the House of Commons. He repeated on the second day of the renewed session the success of the first. He made a most happy, beautiful, inconsequent speech. It was all about the difficu Wes of Ministers in 'dealing with outraged deputation, and anxiety about what is to become of the char- women of the Houses of Parliament, and the Parliamentary scandal of calling the two Houses together in October. There never was a leader of any party who did this kind of thingquite so well. Does anybody ask what was the good of doing it? The reply is that which was given to Peterkin in the poem. Nobody knew what all the _badinage meant. But 'twas glorious badinage.

There are several MINISTERIAL important changes in CHANGES, the constitution of the Ministry which meet Parliament for the Autumn Bitting. Mr. • Churchill and Mr. McKenna have exchanged their respective departments at the Home Office and Admiralty. Lord Carrington who is nearing his three score years and ten, hands over the ever-increasing weight of departmental business at the Board of Agriculture to a young and active colleague. It is the policy of the Liberal Government in making small holdings a real thing and not a Utopian ideal, and se stemming the tide of - rural depopulation, which has made the

work of the Board of Agriculture so heavy. And Lord Carrington has played a con- spicuous and useful part in helping on that policy. His shrewd common sense and genial optimism will still be a valuable element in the Cabinent. Mr. Runciman, who succeeds him, is followed at the Board of Education by Mr. .T. A. Pease, whose good work as I Chief Liberal Whip was rewarded by Ministerial promotion, but whose energy and capacity obviously destined him for a more strenuous post than that of the Chancery of the Duchy of Lancaster. A number of changes in minor posts have also strengthened the effectiveness of the Ministry. Mr. Balfour tried to make a cheap sneer out of the Government's policy of keeping its machinery up to date. The Tory administrations of Lord Salisbury and Mr. Balfour himself were proverbial for sticking in the ruts, and the staleness of "an old gang." No ea° can make such a charge against the Liberal Government.

div.p: iurday October 28, 1911.
NOTES Afin NOTIONS.

"Well, I'M clanged," said Jack Trumpeter to Wm. Hornblower, "here's Mr. Townroe been writing to th" Dispatch ' to say that th' Parr Hall and th' overflow meeting were crowded last week because of National Service."—" Surely, never !" replied William, "doesn't he mention that th' Champion Band were tbeer, at bothplaces? "—" No."—" Well I'll be—." . _

. - Lord Roberts has long been the trump card of the National Service League enthusiasts, but the trump card has been over-trumped. Lord Kitchener is reported to have declared himself a strong supporter of the Territorial movement—which is moving very smoothly and well—and to have also declined emphatically the invitation of Lord Roberts to join the agitation for compulsory. service. "Keep off the track" seems to be the in- genious answer which the Tramways Com- mittee has in pickle for those unfortunate victims of the dangerous setts and uneven metals along the tram route. Alderman Smethurst expressed great confidence at Tuesday's Council Meeting in fighting any claim which came before them, but, he added with a naivete which caused roars of laughter if it is a bad case we will try to settle it." Valour tempered with discretion! • _ •

• " Daylight Saving has received the official approbation of the Town Council, thanks to Alderman Pierpoint's motion, but we fear that more than one member had a hazy notion of what he was voting for. Both Councillors Jenkins and Bellian seemed to be under the impression that their bed-time would be altered. No such time-honoured institutions will be interfered with. Time and events will !remain the same, only the daylight will be more in evidence. * * Mr. Lloyd George, speaking at a meeting of members of friendly societies in London, on Saturday, said that as a result of a series of conferences at the Treasury the worst difficulties in the way of the Insurance Bill had been removed. In his opinion the prospects of the Bill were absolutely safe, and it would be on the Statute Book before Christmas. Explaining the work of the Local Health Committees, the Chancellor said he attached great importance to that part of the scheme. The reports from those committees on the health conditions of fifteen million working-class homes would form a basis on which to build social reform in the future.

• • Our contemporary last week resur- rected a pious resolution,expressing "profound regret at the intended removal from the town of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint " which resolution was passsed at annual meeting of the Conservative Association in February last. We are thus reminded that the Conservatives have not ben entirely unmindful of the great services rendered to their party by the ex-Member. At the same meeting it was also suggested that the freedom of the borough should be conferred upon Mr. Pierpoint, but there was no sug- gestion that the Conservative party should do anything to make Mr. and Mrs. Pierpoint feel at home" in the house of their friends." The honour is now to be conferred by the Council, but it will be a civic honour purely and simply, and does not liquidate the debt of honour of the Conservative party.

There is likely to he at least one happy and unlooked-for sequel to the strik4 troubles in Liverpool. As a result of the restricted opening of public-houses in the city during that trying time there was such a marke i diminution of drunkenness as has impressed itself on the more observant sections of the community. Public opinion has already made itself felt in a remarkable way. On Thursday the Liverpool magis- trates by 49 votes to 24 adopted a report by the Licensing Committee which recommends the closing of public-houses and clubs at 10 o'clock at night and opening not earlier than 8.30 in the morning. Sunday hours are restricted to three in the report, and no woman, or person under 16 years shall be served before noon. This is an astonishingly big "step in the right direction" and if it became law would do much to lessen the worst evils of indulgence in drink. We hope —but have no great confidence—that the Warrington Licensing Committee will follow the example of Liverpool.

- • - The writer in the ?Times" of" A Pilgrim- age of British Farming," writing of Cheshire and Lancashire, thus concludes his remarks on Northern Cheshire:— We left the low land by the 'Mersey and travelled through a succession cf parks and suburbs, until we turn to cross the Mersey at Warrington. There we saw where the smoke came from, for Warrington itself seemed to be dispensing enough black smoke to darken the air of a whole county, while a little further eeaward lay Widnes and Runcorn, where it has been suggested that cast metal trees should be set up, so poisonous is the atmosphere to living ones. But for all the smoke the cultivated land, highly farmed too at that, comes right up to Warrington, and we saw the shadows from the chimney-tops wreathing over good crops of wheat and oats, which appeared to have taken no greatsr harm than a little dinginess of aspsct. There are points of interest in the above for several prominent townsmen who have shown concern in the smoke question. The Mayor will be pleased to learn that the crops are no worse, as supporting his contention that the human lungs do not suffer through the inhalation of factory smoke; Alderman Bennett will find satisfaction from the other point of view, in the suggestion about cast- iron trees; and we would remind Alderman Bolton that he once said that "grass would not grow in Warrington 1"

ASIATIC TO WN-P LANNING. In the course of his opening lecture repo-ted in last Saturday's issue of this paper, Mr. By. It. Aldridge summarised the history of the movement and touched upon modern town-planning achievements in other countries. As China happens just now to be especially to the fore, bulking unusually large in the public eye, I may briefly allude to a report made not very long ago by the American Consul at Hong Kong on the progress of a decidedly significant scheme inaugurated by a number of Chinese capitalists, viz., the construction to order, on the shore of Yehli Bay, of a modern city (to be called Heunchow), with all foreign comfoita. The scheme provided for a well laid-out city, with broad streets and foreign buildings for shops and residences, the whole to be governed by a municipal council. It also provided for schools, charitable institutions, police and fire stations, theatre, peblic gardens, electric light and trams, waterworks, afforestation, chamber of commerce, and free libraries. Opium smoking and gambling of all sorts are to be strictly prohibited. The construc- tion of the city was commenced in 1909, and quite a large number of buildings have been erected. The important fact about this enterprise (says the rerort)i is the desire of the Chinese business men to establish a city upon a modern lines, with all modern improve- manta for their own use and comfort. The whole enterprise indicates a disposition towards modern things which will be of vast importance in the trade of the country in the near future. My own point for the moment is that, if the intensely conservative and often despised Chinese are awaking to the importance
THE REBELLION IN CHINA.

Police Competition for " Hippodrome " Cap. On Friday ri last week the second am.ual shot- putting competition for the above silver cup. presmted to the Force last year, was held in the Police Station yard. The cup is competed for annually, the wiener holding it till next competition. In addition to the cup five prizes were given by the Police Athletic Club. Last year the winner lwas Detective Holland, who on this cceasion was beaten by Constable John Manson, Holland taking second place. The other prize-winners were : —P.C. Cameron, 3rd; P.C. Willis, 4th ; and Detective Craig, sth. FIRE GRATES. If you want a new grate our large and varied stock will interest you.—J. S. GARLAND, Bridge St., Warrington.—Adyt. Drowning Mystery. About SF) on ThurEclay morning the body of a fully clothed woman was seen floating in the Bridge- water Canal between Blackbear Budge and Manor Locks at Latchford, by Miss Alice Frost a dressmaker who resides ate, Manor Locks. She at once informed a look-keeper named Joseph Shaw, who in company with a man named Collins, a carter of Warburton- street, recovered the body from the water. The police afterwards conveyed the body to the mortuary, but up to the time of writing the woman had not been identified. She was a woman about 40 years of age, and sft. 2ies high. An inquest will be held this (Saturday) morning. Warrington Photographic Society. *, At the weekly meeting on Tuesday six of the members (all officers and members of the Committee, by the way) had the pleasure and honour of seeing their own work thrown on the screen. The occasion was the visit of the Lancashire and Cheshire Photo- graphic Union box of slides to the Ac ulemy rooms of Ike above society. Cony abide- Hoes must especially be given to the last named, who is the youngest of the successful workers and to Mr. Frost for his nature study pictures, including the nests of Various birds. S. GARLAND 51, to 55, Bridge st, Warrington.—Adyt. Co-operative Society's Concert. Another large audience was present at the Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening, when the second concert of the session was provided by the " Naval Serenaders," a capable company of artistes. The concert was of a first class order opening with a charming litttle chorus" The Merry Sailors "by the ce.mpany, who also contributed" Red Roses," Your oln Sun Bonnett," and "We could learn to Love." Misa May Valentine sang" Carmena "very effectively while the duet" Sweethearts " by Miss Valentine and Mr. Ogden was a moat popular item. The compusy also gave an excellent rendering of the Miserere Scene Irons" II Trovatote " Mr. George Cameron was a warm favourite with his banjo solos. The humorous aide of the programme was in the capable hands of Mr. Franklyn Taylor who created great merriment with his songs and jokes. The humorous scene Come to the Wedding " by the company, was also the cause for considerable hilarity.

ANTHRACITE STOVES, Boomonictl, clean, cheerful Price from 37/6.—J. S. Clancerm, St, to 35, Bridge at. Warrington.—Advt. "San Toy." The Royal Court Theatre was crowded in every part on Saturday evening when the opera section of , the Warrington Musical Saciety gave their final per- formance of "San Toy." It was an evening of unalloyed pleasure and appreciation, the principals being re-called again and again. The performance went with delightful crispness from beginning to end and reflected credit upon all who had been concerned in a truly memorable production. After the last act, the curtain was again raised and the principals came forward to receive a great ovation. Bouquets and other handume presents were lavished upon them by admirers, some of the gifts being of a novel character. Fel. insane°, Miss Mullins received a small basket which on being opened was found to contain a kitten. Mr. .1. ('anon Bardsley, who had impersonated a British fficer, was presented with a toy rifle. Mr. F. H. Crosaley:(condactor) and Mr. R. Walford Lomas (stage manager and "coach ") were called before the footlights and warmly cheered. " God save the King" was sung, and after the curtain bad fallen the com- pany clasped hands and joined in singing "Auld Lang Syne."

A " Macbeth" Re-anion. A second re-union of those who took part in the production of "Macbeth" was held on Thursday night at the Church Rooms, Trinity Buildings, when Mr. Arthur Browne took the chair, and after making some introductory remarks called upon Dr. Law, who said that the latest proposition was that" Richard the Third" should be played on one night, and "mute Cieser" the other two nights, for the Shakespeare Commemoration for the year 1912, but this was of course subject to the members agreeing and to the committee also agreeing to it from a business point of view. An excellent programme was than none through by Messrs.H. M. Ashton, Harvey Adams, Wheeler, Eric Fairclough, Victor Roberts, Daintitb, Walker. Chester and Houghton, and by the Misses Adams, Tuustall, Bracecamp, Ellison, and Truslove, and most interest- ing excerpts from Shakespeare were given in the individual scenes, sometimes alone and sometimes in duos and trios. Another feature wns an excellent rendering given by Mr. Chedburn, a stranger to the town, who rendered Robert Buchannan's " Era lachimo " Dr. Law of course assisted in several of the scales, and concluced the programme by giving the "Dream Scene " of "Romeo and Murcutio " from " Romeo and Juliet." div.head: National Service League's Sin of
div.p: National Service League's Sin of
Omission.

In our issue of Saturday last, we were pleased to refer to the magnificent reception accorded to the Perfection Soap Works Band, at the meeting of the National Service League. We feel sure that every Warring- tonian is proud of its success. Judge of our surprise, however, when our attention was called to the following correspondence in the "Daily Dispatch," to find- that no single word of praise or credit is given to it by Mr. B. S. Townroe for the crowded meeting. Our thanks are due to Mr. Osborne for publicly rectifying the omission and putting the facts in their true relationship. Mr. Crosfield only last week stated that National Service was becoming a matter of party politics, and judging by this exhibition of "slim " tactics, the charge seems to be sub- stantiated. Fie, Fie, Mr. Townroe ! NATIONAL SERVICE.

To THE EDITOR OF THE "DAILY DISPATCH." Sir,—Many believers in the necessity of national service fear that apathy and ignorance will prove too strong opponents to be overcome before it is too late. The eighth annual meeting of the Warrington Division of the National Service League held yesterday, proves that steady work will conquer these enemies of national efficiency. For this meeting the largest hall in this town, one which only the biggest speakers succeed in filling, was engaged, and Lord Derby promised to preside at 8 p.m. By 7.15 this great hall was packed, and an overflow meeting was immediately advertised. This also was crowded by 7.40 p.m., and we then had to turn hundreds away. This enthusiasm, and the numerous adherents won over by Lord Derby's straight speaking on the subject of the Territorial force, seems to prove that the tide is turning, and national service will soon be regarded as one of the questions of the day.
B. S. TOWNROE. 10. Winmarleigh street, Warrington.

'October 19th: A NATIONAL SERVICE METING. To THE EDITOR OF THE "DAILY DISPATCH." Sir,—There is a serious omission from the letter of Mr. B. S. Townroe in your issue of to-day. It is quite true that the largest hall in Warrington was packed at 7.15 p.m., although Lord Derby was not advertised to preside until 8 p.m. Whilst I have no desire to minimise the importance of a meeting which the noble lord had promised to address, yet, in fairness to the winners of the recent brass band contest at the Crystal Palace, it should have been pointed out that they had promised to play. The invitation cards included the following: "The Warrington Male Voice Choir and the Apollo Choir will sing and Messrs. Crosfield's Band will play from 7 to 8 p.m." Mr. Townroe's zeal for the League may have been res- ponsible for the omission. EDMUND OSBORNE. 22, Bold-street, Warrington, October 20th.
