div.head: MR. A H. CROSFIELD AT HAMPSTEAD Address on Music.
div.p: MR. A H. CROSFIELD AT HAMPSTEAD Address on Music.

.. - Mr. A. H. Crosfield. on Saturday evening, delivered what he described as his maiden speech on music at a concert at the Hamp- stead Garden Suburb. The speaker illustrated his points in some clever performances on the piano. Music, he said, is as delightful and as elusive as the scent of the flower or the lustre of the brilliant. Throughout the ages man had recognised the power of music, and when he mentioned the value of music as a source of inspiration to the soldier when he went, into battle, he hoped he would not be sus- pected of bellicose tendencies, 'seeing that he came from a long line of Quaker ancestry. He regarded music as something wlikh was capable of expressing the " inexpressible." Huxley had called literature the most endur- ing form of refined pleasure, but he (the speaker) thought that, in point of beauty, most people would give music the palm, be- cause so much of the music we had had drawn _

its inspiration from Nature. Where, it seemed to him, music even exceeded and excelled the beauties of Nature itself was in its power to express human emotion and human feeling. This was a thought which would occur to most on hearing the soprano solo " Jerusalem " in Mendelssolin's "St. Paul "—a marvellous illustration of music conveying the words and the pathetic idea of the song. Again, in " Elijah " we got to an extraordinarY extent the idea of pleading and prayer. And what a series of striking contrasts were furnished in the music of the philosophic Each, the magnifi- cent Wagner, and the greatest of all corn, posers, Beethoven. Mr. Crosfield's address was interrupted several times by the applause of an apprecia- tive audience. The concert was a arratsuccess, both artistically and in other ways. Mrs. Crosfielcl to* the leading_ part at the piano in the overture t) " fannhauser,'' and in Schumann's beautiful and interesting quintette. In both her tette and brilliant mo- tion delishud the entire audience, while her play- ing of that extremely difficult, characteristic, and striking piece of Lit zee, the "Rh a psodie Hoogroise," was simple superb and armed immense enthusiasm. B.,th in the orchestral pieces and in her solo, Miss Elliadi's playing on the violin was also greatly admired. The quality: strength and fulness of tone were much marked in sl young a player, and with her gate she should go far in her musical carter. Mr. Henry Vivian, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield (mho hart at ranged the concert with the object of redwing funds for the organ which is to be erected in the new Free Church at Hampstead Garden Suburb), said that lie possessed a photograph which had been taken at the cutting of the first sod on the Co-partnership Estate, and Mr. Crosfield's figure occupied a very prominent position at that ceremony. He was delighted to see him there after four years to see how much had been accomplished. Mr. Crosfield hail given them a magnificent musical treat, with the assistance of Mrs. Crosfield and their coadjutors. (Applause).

MEAN THEFTS FROM LITTLE CHILDREN. BENCH COMMEND POLICE SMARTNESS. . _

_ An intereeting case was heard at the Borough Court on Saturday before Mr. J. W. Hayward as the presid- ing magistrate, alien three charges were preferred against Thomas Jenks, 58, Priestley-street of stealing money to the amount of 305., while Thomas Lang- lawn, of no settled abode, a clerk, was charged with siding and abetting—Both pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable said that for some weeks past the police bad been receiving on an average from two to three reports a week of money being stolen from children of tender years. From 15 to 20 constables had been placed on special duty to keep obsertation in different parts of the town. The thefts were from children of workingclass parents who bad been sent upon errands. They were stopped in the streets and decoyed to a remote place and then robbed. The parents hed suffered considerably and could ill afford to spare the money, in several instances having to go without their meals through the robberiee. A descrip- tion of the man who bad been committing the thefts was given to the police with the result that on the 13th inst. P.C. Whitby observed the prisoner who tallied with the description. He kept him under observa- tion and upon his arrival in Sankey-street pt isoner was also observed by Detective Holland who had with him ahoy who bad been robbed. The boy identified prisoner as the thief. Prisoner was at once arrested and taken to the Police Station when in reply to the charge he immediately replie ; "if you will allow me 1 will makes clean breast of everything,l am sick of it." He also implicated the other prisoner who, when arrested, admitted receiving Is. 63. as half of the subject of the first charge. Jenks admitted sinriler thefts on nine different occasions. Jeoks stated that he had been brought down to that level be his wife. Longhorn had nothing to soy. Previous convictions having been proved against both prisoners, Jerks was sentenced to six months' hard labour and Longhorn to two months' hard labour. The Chairman said that the Bench would like to commend Dateatire Holland and P.C. Whitby for their smartness in apprehending the prisoner Jerks. DOMESTIC SERVANT IN TROUBLE. COMMITTED TO ,THE SESSIONS. At an Occasional Court held on Tuesday, before Mr. T. Baxter, Minnie Birkenhead, alias LeviniaMilliegton, was charged with obtaining by false preencea a lady's bicycle, value .£5, the property of Bessie Clarke, on June 7th. Bessie Clarke, housekeeper at Dutton Park Farm, Dutton, said that on the day in question the prisoner called to see her at 10 a.m. and said that her mother wanted to know if witness would lend her sister Emma her bicycle to go to Winsford. She stated that her mother would pay for the loan of it, but witness said that she did not want any money so long as the bicycle was brought back in good condition. As the prisoner did not return the bicycle witness went to see her sistw Emma who denied sending for the bicycle, as also did the prisoner's mother. Information was given to the police. Annie Fowles. a single women, reekl:ng with her parents at Lane-ena Farm, Rudheath, stated that at 10.43 p.m. on Jose 7th she was standing at the heck gate of the house ashen the prisoner came up with the bicycle. She at first went past witness into the yard and did not speak, but upon a itness telling her to be careful of the dog, she replied that she had received permission at the front of the house to leave the bicycle there. She also stated that Me would call about ten o'clock the next morning for it, as it was badly punctured. This was no unusual occurrence, as People frequently left bicycles at the house and called later for them. She could not identify the prisoner, as it was dark at the time, but she could identify the Ticycle (produced) as being the one that was left at the

- _ bons. Prisoner was then charged with stealing a lady's bicycle and a lady's coat, value £2 19r., the property of her mo' her, Harriet Millington, on the 13th inst. Evidence was given to the effect that prisoner called at her mother's house, and by telling her that someone wanted to see her "Very particularly," got her to go out for half an hour. When she returned, prisoner had left, and the bicycle and coat were missing. P.C. Cotterill stationed at Preston Brook. spoke to charging the prisoner in loth instances but she did not reply. Mite Wright at %those home the prisoner bad been living, sqid she bad known the prisoner for five years. During the whole of that time the prisoner had been csrrying to a succession of thefts. She did not think a voluntary home could keep her, but that she would be better in a Government home. Prisoner was committed to the Chester Quarter Sessions, the Chairman remarking that he hoped that she would be placed in a home where she would reform.

A PRISONER'S INTMYTIONS.—John O'Brien, a labourer, of no r ettled abode, was charged on remand with loiter- ing in Sankey-street with intent to commit a felony.— P.C. Edwards raid that shortly after 11.40 p m. on Sunday the Bth inst, he noticed the prisoner acting in a ruspicions manner in Senkey.s.reet. He was walking from Dixon-street to Baldistreet examining the shop doors, lie afterwards went into the doorway of a tobacconist's shop where witness found him in a crouching position. On being questioned, prisoner amid: 'You have been too sharp for me, I meant to have a 'pop' at the jeweller's shop. I would have broken one of the windows at the back." Prisoner now raid he was drunk at the time. Ile was looking for n place to sleep in, as he had nowhere to go. The Chief Constable : He is an habitual "cadger." Three previous convictions having been proved against him, prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. DRUNKENNESS.—Two cases of drunkenness with dis- orderly behaviour were also dealt with. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Bolton, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. H. Thornton, S. Wright, W. Roberts, W. Furness, G. Pilling and T. Locker. CHARGE OF FAMILY NEGLECT.—WEILGI LONGIII, 13, Melville-street, was charged with neglecting his four children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary angering and injury to health.—Mr. A. Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., said that the case had been under the supervision of the Society's officers for a considerable time. The husband was warned and for a time had made an impression, I ut he broke down again. He could earn from 40s. to 454. a week ass rivetter, but he would not work and spent what money he could upon drink, leaving his wife and children without food and clothing. But for the help of the neighbours the children would undoubtedly have starved. He had been warned many times by the Society. During the last three weeks the wife and children had had nothing to rat but dry bread.— Prisoner said that be would promise to get a new home together and mend his ways.—The Bench adjourned the case for two months to give prisoner a chance of amending his ways. MARKET THEFT.—Sarnuel Houghton, of no nettled abode, was charged with stealing a nickel-plated spoon from a stall in the market. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was seen loitering about the stalls in the Market-place and afterwards he was offering a nickel- Plated spoon for sale in Lyme-street. He only asked 14d. for it. Detective Clough questioned the prisoner with regard to having the spoon in his possession and he stated that he had bought it from a stall in the market. The cries? was not satisfied, however, and took him to the Polies Station where he admitted the theft. Prisoner said he was drunk at the time and when in drink he had no control over himself. Twelve previous convictions having been proved prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. LODGER'S AGGRAVATE) ASSADLT.—Edorard Mullin, I, Dolman's-lane, was charged with committing an aggravated assault upon Catherine Corfleld. He pleaded guilty, with great provocation. The Chief Constable said that the prisoner lodged with the prosecutor at the above address. About eleven o'clock the previous night the prisoner, who was in the house, Gegto to make a row. The proceutrix went to quieten him, when the prisoner deliberately struck her in the eve, inflicting a nasty wound which had to be stitched it the Infirmary. A smoke consumer and fuel economiser, said to be the result of twenty years' trials, has been successfully tested at Sheffield. Coal w.mi fed into the furnace of a boiler generat- rig steam for running the works, with the w.ual result—the emission of black smoke from the chimney; then the consumer was ;int iiito action, and in place of the black smoke there was orly a slight trace of the products of combusbion. The change as effected by an arrangement of a series of de- vices so iikaced in the flues as to intercept the smoke, and cause it to be ignited by the flames. Two air circulators are so placed as to allow the desired quantity of external air to be circulated awing these deices, causing the smoke to be propcily ignited. and con- burned around thc boiler flues before entering the chimney.

TUF.SDAY.—Before CountiHors 11 Roberts (in the chair), C Jackson Holmes, Messrs .1 Rymer Young, T Locker, W Richardson and Colonel Edelsten. WORKING HORSE IN UNFIT STATE.—John Cobley, Town Pit, Whitley, a teamsman, was charged with cruelly illtreeting a horse by working it in an unfit state. He pleaded not guilty. Inspector Dee, of the R S.P.C.A., said that at 10 a.m. on the 12th inst. be saw a boy named Vernon in charge of a horse attached to a curt, in Arpley-road. Tee horse was exceedingly lame. There Wen an old wound on the right fore leg. He afterwards visited the defendant who admitted that the horse was in a rather poor condition. Defendant said that he was at work when the horse was taken out without his ,knowledge. Defendant was tined 10a. and costs (19s). A JUVENILE'S THEFT.--At a Juvenile Court immediately after the business of the above court, Thomas Dibble aged 14, Ming with his mother at 2, Berrys-3ard, was chargeu ot reraszd with steuliog 42 rabbit skins from a box in the market, the property of William Chapman, on the 14th inst. The Chief Constable said that the case had been adjourned in order to make further inquiries. Although the boy had never appeared before the magletretes previously, the police had good foundation to laclieve that he had been in the habit of pilfering. During the time he had been in the detention room he had given the police a great deal of trouble, turning the lights on stone o'clock in the morning. The Bench ordered the boy to receive six strokes with the birch rod, the Chairman remarking that this would be his last chance, for if be was brought before the Magistrates again he would be committed to a Reformatory school until he was 19 years of age.

WRDNICSDAY.—Before Mr Chsrles White (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor C Jackson Holmes, Messrs W T Williams and J W Hayward. A GUARDIAN'S NEGLICT.—Kate Marsh Mannion, 98, Foundry-street, was charged under the Children's Act, with neglecting and ill-Ire ding four children of whom she was the guardian. Mr. A. Browne who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. said that the mother of the children had been dead about ton years. The father entered the Workhouse about three years ago and the family thereupon agreed between themselves to keep on the house with the defendint in charge. The three elder brothers contributed 365. a week and the rent of the house was 3s. Bd. a week. Some time ago, however, the defendant gave way to driuk and had neglectA and ill-trestei the children to such an extent thst ou one occasion the doctor had to be called in to see one whom she had ill-treated. On another occasion she nearly strangled one of the young boys, an elder brother having to pull her away. She had also sold a dresser and other articles of furniture. The Society's officers had frequently warned her. Prisoner was aunt to gaol for two months' with hard labour. TRURSDAY.—Before Mr W Roberta (in the chair) and Dr Nadel).

FOUND ON ENCLOSED PREMISES.—John Boyle, 182, Winwick-road, was charged with being found on the enclosed premises of 51, Wilson Patten-street, with intent to commit a felony.—The Chief Constable said than at 7 p.m.on the previonsday P.C.Berry bad occasion to visit the above premises, which were under the charge of the police, when he noticed a light in one of the bedrooms. Information was sent to the Police Station for assistance, at.d a key was obtained. The door of the room where the light was observed was locked, but after a considerable time an entrance was effected, and the prisoner was discovered under the bed. Be had no right to be in the house.—Two pre- vious convictions hiving been proved against him, prisoner was lined 20e and costs, or one month's imprisonment. GAS METER Tugm—Michael Callaghan, a labourer of no settled abode, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Priestley-street, with stealing 6s. from a gas meter at 11, Union-street, and also with wilfully damaging the meter to the estent of 161.—The Chief Constable said that on Monday morning, the 21st mat, prisoner went to the above address and asked if he could have a lie down, which he was permitted to do. Shortly afterwards it was discovered that the meter had been broken int) and the stoney stolen. Prisoner had been spending a lot of money, all of which was in coppers. The meter was absolutely beyond repair. There were 55 previous convictions against the prisoner who was sent to gaol for three months._ _

The complainant slid that he complained to the defendant about his language in Ship-yard when defeniant Wink hint across the eye three times with a stick causing a nasty wound which bad to be trotted at the Infirmary. Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days.

YOUTH'S ATTEMPTED SEIEII/E.—William Ridyard, aged 16, residing with his parents at 698, Koutaford- road, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by severing an artery in his left wrist. Inspector IFoster said Snit about 4 a.m. on the 14th inst. he found the prisoner in the saddle room of Messrs. Magion's stables in Arpley-street in a sta.e of collapse His left hand was in his trousers pocket and hie arm was satur- ated with blood. Prisoner at first stated that he had fallen upon some glass, but afterwards admitted thst he had severed an artery with a razor. The wrist was 155 very bad state and after receiviag attention prisoner was conveyed to the Infirmary where be was detained. It appeared that the father of the prisoner had thrashed him because he stated that be had list some money, which statement the father did not believe. On his promisMg not to attempt the rash act again the case was adjourned until the last Friday in the year. FOOD AND LODGING BY FALSE PRICTENCES.—NeviIIe Roberts, a moulder, of no settled abode, was charged with obtaining food and lodging to the value of 4s. by false pretences, from Mrs. Matilda Bond, 9 Admiral- street. The Chief C3ustable said that on August 29th the prisoner agreed to pay 9s. a week to the complainant stating that he was employed at Hutchings Tannery. A short time afterwards he stated that he was going to work at lipylors and asked the complainant to go to the tannery his wages. She did so and found that the prisoner was not known there. Ile then disappeared and did not return. Prisoner was wanted at Ise or sin other places and he was quite willing to accede to an adjournment so that he could clear the whole matter up. The Bench adjourned the case for seven days.

Spiritualist Lyceum Anniversary. Services in celebration of the anniversary were held in the Druid's Hall on Sunday. At an "open session" in the afternoon the Lyceumists went through the ordinary proceedings of a session—the singing of hymns, silver and golden chain recitations, musical reading, marching and calisthenics, and a number gave some interesting recitations and " pearls." An address was also given by Mr. John Henley, of Man- chester. In the evening the platform was filled with Lyceumists, and a very interesting service was con- ducted by Mr. Stout, the address being given by Mr. Henley. Special suitable hymns were sung, and recitations were ably given by the Misses Eva Fox, Maggie Randle, Lily Llewellyn, Lizzie Cross Land, Mona Archer, and Master Randles. Mr. Herbert Foster was the organist at Ixtth services.

The Examiner, Sa fly October 289 1911• THE WHIP ;N WARRINGTON. A PLAY WITH FORTY TONS OF SCENERY, ar. The Whip is the name r f Lord Branchester's famous thoroughbred, and it gives the title to the drams, because it is around the fortunes of this horse, and the race for the 2000 Guineas for which it is entered, that the story revolves. S me idea of the realism attained in this drama may be gathered from the following description, which appeared in one of the London papers :—"lf you wish to catch a glimpse of the great annual horse glow, at Olympia, if you would like a stroll through the Chamber of Horrors at Madame Tussaud's, if you would see an express steaming at full speed across country, now thundering past wood and meadow, now disappearing into the dark recesses of • gloomy tunnel, and if you would take your place on the grand stand at Newmarket amid a crowd of notabilities and distinguished people, you can accomplish all this by the simple 'mans of booking seats for 'The Whip.'" No less than forty tons of scenery, together with racehorses and otter bounds, ore toured with this production, the transport of which from town to town in itself necessitaos ~me very special arrangements being made. In fact a special train and an army of carpanters, joiners, slagemen, j Ickeye and stable-lids are carried, in addition to a full cimpany of specially selected artiste,.
MISS ELSIE WOOD, MISS MARY NAPIER, siho plays Lady Diana in' The Whip." who plays Lady in '' The Whip." THE WHIP WALTZ

WONDERFUL STAGE REALISM. The first productioa in Wartingtoa next week of " The Whip " will be the chief event of the autumn season. This highly exciting play created a great sensation at the Drury Lane Theatre, where it ran for many months, and those who saw it in London or have since seen it in the provinces speak of it in terms of unstinted praise. Mr. George Dance, who has brought to Warrington some of the best attractions seen hero of recent years, including " Our kiss Gibbs" and "Miss Rook of Rolland," is prodacing " The Whip " in most elabprate fashion, some of the finest effarts at realism ever seen on the stage being included. A racecourse scene is presented in which the horses not only appear but actually race. The spectators witness a wild gallop to the winning post. This effect is managed by a trio f revolving stages on which the horses stand. The climax of the drama is reached with a railway scene A train with passengers erected behind the footlights by a clever device is represented on its journey ; then part of it is unloosed by the villain of the play and left on the line. While it stands there an engine suddenly bursts out of a tunnel at the rear and there is a terrible smash as the curtain descends.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Card Parties.—The Americans are great in going to extremes, no matter what it is, and we rend that scores of Society women, at a fashionable reeort in New Jersey, have been arrested for engaging in card parties in their own homes. According to the American news- papers, half of the prominent residents were "out on bail." The most popular card game there is the "euchre drive," which the Public Prosecutor has declared to be a gambling game. There are not a few who could like to see our authorities take similar action with respect to "whist drives" which, now that the winter is coming on, are once more the chief attraction for social afternoons and evenings. It is no doubts pity that no many women with leisure on their hand, cannot find anything more useful to do than to spend their afternoons in card playing, but if this were taboo, it would shut down on a lot of entettainine, and, RS a rule, the ordinary social card party in harmless enough. It looke, however, as if the police intended to put down the public "drives," which were very popular last winter, and no doubt the charity whist drive, mostly associated with church purposes, will share the same fate. .

A Tip-Ridden Nation.—Like most other classes, the waiters and waitresses sus discontented with their lot, and they have been agitating in London to secure an adequate wage and the abolition of the tipping system. One hardly knows if they are quite sincere in the latter demand, but, as a tip-ridden nation we should all be glad if they succeeded in its accomplishment. At most hotels and restaurants, dinner-table tips are expected at the rate of about 2s lathe £ on the amount of the bill, with a minimum according to circumstances and a visit to ones friends or relatives, usually involves a considerable expense in tips to porters, servants and no on. On this score alone, many a poor i clergyman has been compelled to regard an nvitation to stay with his Bishop as beyond his means. But the doueeur tax is even worse in America and on the Con- tinent, the guest after dining out is expected to seek the kitchen and reward the cook, a thing not usual in this country unless the visitor stays over-night. We may also comfort ourselves with the retlaction that bad as things are, they used to be worse, so many an old- time winter has left on record. A striking example was afforded by Lord William Russell, who was beheaded for high treason in 1683. "He asked," wrote Bishop Burnet who attended him after his sentence," what he should give the executioner. I told him ten gni neas.l He said with a smile, it was a pretty thing to give a fee to have his head cut off.' .

Simple Fare —The apple dumpling, we are told, is food in perfection, not only for the young, but also for the old, and it is suggested that the present time of high prices would be a lgood opportunity for many people given to rich living, Ito economise by resorting to the simpler kind of meals. Many people, in fact, are seriously thinking of taking up vegetarianism on that account, and there in little doubt that vast numbers who over-indulge themselves with flesh foods could do that, at least for a time, with advan- tage to their health and pocket. Sir Thomas Crosby, the newly-elected 81-year-old Lord Mayor of London, speaking with a medical experience of sixty years, Nays that the secret of youthful old age is to keep the arteries young. In youth they are supple and elastic, but harden with a.lvancing years, when the heart has to work at high pressure to perform its functions, and is sooner worn out by being overtaxed. There is no specific against this degeneration, but medical opinion agrees that the hardening of the arteries is hastened by over-indulgence in a meat dietary. Undoubtedly most people of such habits, who are past their youth, would benefit both in health, and in appear- ance, by becoming more or lesa vegetarians, at any rate for a time.

Childrens Services.—That was a bold proves] which was advanced at the Sabbath School Conference in Edinburgh, to the effect that the morning service should be given up entirely to children. The sugges- tion is scarcely likely to be adopted by many churches although there are ninny advantages in bolding services exclusively for children, and attempts to provide for adults and children at the same time have generally , failed, no far as the adults are concerned. In many places, the difficulty is met by a service, say at 930 for children, and at 11 for adults, and although it would be an undue strain upon any one man to conduct two such services consecutively, still the solution seems quite practicable where there is sufficient help, and has in fact proved to be generally successful. Concerning Furs.—With the perceptible shortening of the day., ones thoughts naturally revert to furs, and the question whether the long coney, and other seal coats will be as popular thit, as last winter, is agitating the minds of many possessors of these handsome and comfortable garments. Trimmed fur coats, Fashion has decreed, shall be the rule for the coming season, but this need not cause the owners of the latter to despair, since the long garment can be brought up-to-date by the addition of a hood of some contrasting fur. But

many women will elect to caper their long coats as they are, and very wisely so, sinc• they require no trimming, being quite handsome in themselves. A feature of fashion in peltry will however be the trimming of one fur, with one or more contrasting pelts. In some instances as many as four different kinds of fur have been combined in one garment, and the effect is in each case good, due in part to the richness of the pelts, end in part to the judicious choice of the combining furs. Caracul kid will enjoy much popularity this winter, for it lends itself admirably to combinations with white furs and sometimes it is seen to great advantgge in conjunction I with coarse black Irish crochet. A very charming 'revival that promises to be much in evilence is the early Victorian pelerine in white Russian ermine, encrusted with miniver spots. This is for those women who can afford the luxury ; for others with only modest means less expensive furs will be used. This pelerine has long stole ends cut equate, and sometimes embroidered in snutache. A granny muff of moderate dimensions completes this quaintly becoming garment or it can scarcely be called an accessory. Styles and Fabrics.—There is a den i led effort on the part of dressmakers and designers to break up the straight lines to which we have grown so accustomed, and this effort is no far more pronounced in the styles of afternoon and evening gowns, on which loose draperies and fi3hus, trimmings of fringes and niches— for the greater part arranged in diagonal lines—tend to destroy the silhouette, and to replace it with the styles of 1820, which filled the gap between the seconp Empire and the early Victorian periods. Walking dresses however are till straight although unobtru- sively viler than at this time last year. Black velvet and velveteen were never more popular, It dominates us, and this is not no surprising when we consider that it becomas women of all ages alike, end that its softening effect lends a lustre to the eve of youth, and adds a beauty to skin and hair whilst it takes years off an elderly woman's age. Ile coat and skirt of black velvet bide fair to he as popular this year as last. The touch of black so characteristic of the French designer, and introduced no cleverly into the brightest coloured scheme of dres3, is a dominant note of English fashion also. Great latitude is allowed in the matter of sleeves which man he to elbow, or to wrist, and many have from the elbow, the Tudor puff, the Marie Antoinette frill or the giant bell of 1860. The shoulder line, accompanying all sleeves is plain and flat and square. Sloping shoulders ere not becoming, nor do they euit the temperament of the present generation of women.

div.head: DANGEROUS NEGLECT.
div.p: DANGEROUS NEGLECT.

There are many men and women who do not realise how serious it is to neglect pains in the loins and back, urinary disorders, gravel, puffiness in the ankles and under the eyes, and rheumatic twinges. These and other unmistakable symptoms of kidney and bladder trouble are due to the kidneys failing to filter the urinous poisons out of the blood. The Warrington Auxiliary of the British and Foreign Bible Society has this week been celebrating it centenary. "Bible Sunday" was observed in many places of worship on Sunday last and ref:rence eras made by the preachers to the great work of the society in circulating the Scriptures all over the world. The chief feature of the celebration, however, was the great public meeting held in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening when the speakers were the Lord Bishop of Chester (Right Rev. Dr. Jayne), and the Rev. F. W. Macdonald (sx-Pretident the Wesleyan Conference). The Yen. Archdeacon Madden was also announced to speak, but wrote regretting his inability to attend. There was a large and representative audience and on the platform were clergy and nainiatere of many denomina- tions. A united choir drawn from the various places of worship was also in attendance and, in addition to leading the singing of the hymn, gave inspiring inter- pretations of the anthem "Send out Thy Light" (Gonnod), and the Hallelujah Chorus (Handel). Mrs. Arthur Booth sang " Hear Ye, Israel" (Mendelisohn), and the duet " Love divine" was given by Mrs. Arthur Booth and Mr. J. H. Draper. The musical arrangements were in the hands of Mr. F. M Darby. Mug. Bac., and Mr. W. H. Payton, Mac Bar. The Rector (Rev Canon With' presided and amongst others p-esent were : The Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph), the Revs Hon C F Cross, E C E Carleton, H B Firth, H H Corsbie, G C Briggs, J Davies, F C Shirtcliff, J R Jonss, A J Brett, J Collins, J H Garnett, J 0 Haughton (district secretary of the society), W A Beckett, E Morgan, H Middlewood, H Williamson, Joseph Howard, H Ogden and W Mrs T H Lyon, Mrs Garnett, Mrs Dodds, Miss Bessie Dutton, Messrs C E Parker, S P Silcock, J C Holland, W H Stanefield, John Fairclough. Seger Owen, E Wynne Jones. II J Westbrook, A Mounueld, W T Williams and G Wallington. Prayer was offered by the Rev. W. Rea

div.head: SLACKENING OF INTEREST.
div.p: A SLACKENING OF INTEREST.

The Rev. J. HAUGHTON,iii an introductory statemmt, pointed out that the present trio of secretaries of the branch (the Revs. E.C.E. Carleton and John Yonge and Mr S P Silcock) bad worked together for the past twenty-one yearn—a service of which anyone might well be proud. (Applause) The auxiliary had been greatly indebted to Mr. E. J. Guest who Lir many years collected ell the subscriptions. (Applause.) When he retired in 1890, a new principle was adopted, lady collectors being appointed on behalf of each place of worship. During the first fifty years of the existence of the mediate, Warrington'e annusl contribution to the funds of the Bible Society averaged £37, but during the lest fifty years it had fallen to £54. It would therefore appear that while Warrington had been grow- ing, interest in the work of the society had been slackening. They wanted the Centecary celebrations ! to be a new jumping-off mark for greatly extended work. 'rney wanted, if possible, to have an annual , meeting in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The work of the , society was a great and noble one, binding all Christian men and women together in a common cause. , Applause). A MEMORABLE YEAR. The tacit:oft said the British and Foreign Bible , Society was the fourth of five great societies which were I founded about the Eighteenth Century. The first was I the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge, I in 1898 ; the second the Society for the Propagation I of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, in 1701 ; the third, the i Church Missionary Society, n 1799 ; the fourth, the I British and Foreign Bible Society in 1801 ; and the ! fifth the National Society in 1811. This was a very memorable year, for it marked the tercentenary of the publicatios of the authoriaed version of the Bible. They all felt what a deep debt of gratitude they owed to the translators of the Scriptures. Nothing could ever equal the grandeur of the langusgeof theauthorieed version, and although, perhape, its accuracy might be discounted to a certain extent by the rev:sed version made thirty years ago, nothing could ever take its place ; its language and its rhythm were so beautiful. Referring to the work of the British and Foreign Bible Society, the Rector said 229,000,000 copies of Holy Scripture had been published during the last 100 years, at a cost of £16,000,000, in 432 different Marines, 115,000,000 of those copies being In English. They most all feel that the society was fulfilling that wonderful prophecy in Isaiah, that " the earth shall he full of the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters corer the see," and that in supporting it they were obeying that great and almost , last command of our Lord, to 'go into all the world ! and preach the Gospel to every creature." They ought to show their gratitude to the society by contributing as liberally as they could, no that the offering from that branch to the parent society might be aomething like £lOO. (Applause). A WONDERFUL CENTURY. THE AWAKENING OF THE EASTERN RACES. _ .

The Rev. F. W. MACDONALD, Who Dist treated his tubject from the historical standpoint, said it spoke worlds for the excellent constitution of the Bible Society that it bad survived the nineteenth century, which was a very trying one for all manner of institu- tions. Principles, traditions, habits, modes of thought, and ideals went down one after another in a long aeries during the nineteenth century. There had been cen- turies singularly barren in respect of great events or striking personalities, and they counted for very little in the annals°, the human race. They could not say that of the nineteenth century. lie believed that as that century receded into historic distance, there would be general agreement that there had only been some two or three centuries in the history of the world more filled with incidents of a far-couching ' character. (Applause.) Not only had the art., industrial and commerce of the civilized world been altogether reorganized, not only had the bounds of knowledge, more particularly in respect of science and the mechanical arta, been immensely widened, but there had been changts in almost every department of human life. The whole area had been swept by winds from every point of the compass. Philosophy, theology, social thought, the theories of life that pre- vailed—some had been destroyed, others had been changed almisat out of recognition, others bad been reborn, cast in new moulds and net out upon new lines of progress. It had been a
CENTURY OF IMMENSE DESTEDCTION AND OF MOST

div.head: PREGNANT RE-CONSTRUCTION.
div.p: PREGNANT RE-CONSTRUCTION.

...--...... For any net of principles for any institution or any organised and definite plan of work to have survived that century was an admirable note of vitality and health on its part. The Bible Society to-day was fully alive. (Applause) The principles and ideals that governed the formation of the society and sent it oct upon its MIESiOII were still the ideals and principles by which it was inspired and directed. ilvey were living principles, lodged in living human souls, and the aims ideals and methods of the society sprang directly out of strong, fresh, ever-renewed Chrietiau life and faith. (Applause.) They could look the new century in the face with more hops and cotfidence with regard to the future of the Bible Society than they could in the case of institutions which he would not be no impolite as to mention. Without dwelling upon any of the lee. happy end rearisuring Cigna which it would be possible to discover, he thought the most striking characteristic of the Christian Church to-day was that the eviabgelisa- tion of the world had been laid afresh upon its heart. The speaker proceeded to show how races which were once secluded were now being trought into the full current of civilized life. For ages
CHINA. AND J. -APAN

I had clung to their isolation and shrunk fr..m the embarrassing attentions of the West. div.head: INVASION DANGER.
div.p: INVASION DANGER.
War Office Has " Enough Money For Everything.'

Mr. F. D. Acland, Financial Secretary cf the War Office, made an interesting speech on Saturday evening at Tiverton, where he bad earlier in the day opened a new Liberal Club. Having stated that the British Government were doing their beat to see that the Turco-Itatian war did not spread and involve other nations, he said : "My buainese is with one of those Departments concerned with the preparations for war. We have now provided in every way, so that within forty-right hours of an alarm being given the Terri- torial Force could stand forth absolutely equipped for everything it might have to face in any iuvasion or sudden emergency. I know also that the other day when we were—se every country always must be— seeing that onr house was in order, seeing what would happen if war arose on a large scale when I asked my military colleagues on the Army Council it they wanted more money for any purpose they sad No. We have enough money for everything we require.' Jam sore that would never have been said before in the whole history of the British Army. If our Navy were to be deetroyed, as now it cannot, it would not be necessary for any foreign country to send one single men to invade this country, because we should be starved into surrender even if we had an army of ten million men absolutely equipped in • tip-top way. In such a case all the invaders would bare to do would be to send one man with terms of peace, and we should have to accept them in order to get our own corn :ships through. All authorities—and leaders of the great political parties—agree that the greatest invading force that could be got into this country would be 100,000 men. So long as we maintain our Territorial Force in a state of real efficiency we should be able to give a good account of a force of that sort.'

div.head: ROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: ROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
fly Philip Snowden, II P. THE RAILWAY COMMISSION
REPORT.

There is only one word I can think of to describe the Report of the Railway Commis- sion. It is staggering. I doubt if anybody —even a railway director—ever for one moment dreamt that the Commissioners would issue such a Report. If Lord Claud Hamilton hai drawn up the Report it could not have given the railway trade unions less than this Report gives them. The whole thing is so amazing that one's mind is filled with all kinds of thoughts about what it means, and what is behind it, and how it came to pass, and what is going to happen. I think I understand the reason why the railwaymen have been—well, I will say dis- appointed—every time they have trusted to political leaders, but one hesitates to say things which are true but which are difficult to prove by documentary evidence. Motives never are put into written or verbal agree- ments. But the real truth is that the railwaymen have been sacrificed every time to political interests. It was so in 1907; it was so in August; it is so in regard to this Report. The whole proceedings in regard to the collapse of the railway strike last August were prompted by consideration for the interests of politicians. WHAT THE MEN WANT.

, The railwaymen want recognition of their union. In that demand they are .right. My antipathy to strikes, except as a last resort, is well known. But refusal to recognize unionism is the highest justification for a strike, because without recognition we can- not have the machinery for the settlement of disputes. The strike last August was for the recognition ot the union. The strike was called off because it was believed, or at least it was said, that the Commission to be appointed would without doubt recommend the recognition of the union. Indeed one prominent individual boasted that the Government, under pressure from the men, had " packed " the Commission so as to ensure a Report which would give the men everything they wanted. It is time some of the railwaymen's leaders stopped fooling the men. They fooled the men in 1907 by making. .them believe

that the Agreement which had been forced upon them was a good thing and gave recog- nition of the union, while every impartial person who examined it knew that it would never work, and that it did not recognise the union in any shape or form. The abortive strike last August ended in the retreat Of the men at the call of the Executive. The men were told that the union had been recognised because a railway director had spoken to a union man at the office of the Board of Trade. I wrote after the collapse of the strike a very restrained article because I hoped that the Report of the Commission might do something to justify the surrender which the Executive made. The facts connected with the " settlement " of that strike were such as to justify vigorous language. But I preferred to wait to see if the disaster of that surrender could be redeemed by the report of the Commission. But now we know the report, and it completes the humiliation of the surrender last August. NO RECOGNITION.
_ . Let us have no self deception, or attempt& to deceive others about the terms of this
Report. The bald truth is that it does not give the recognition of the union in any shape or form. The point which some of the papers are making that. there is a recogni-
tio'n of the union 10-y the fact that the Men's secretary can be. elected from outside, is too _ _ _
absurd or words. There is not a trace of the recognition of the union there. We are . .

told that there is nothing to prevent the men from electing an official of the union to the position. Of course there isn't. There is nothing in the Conciliation Scheme to pre- vent every one of the men's representatives on the Boards from being members of the union, and as a matter of fact most of them are. But is that recognition of the union ? It is nothing of the sort. Recognition of the union means that the union as an organisa- tion shall be recognised, and the officials shall
have the right to confer with the company in the name of and on behalf of the union men.
THE SPIRIT OF THE REPORT.

The free choice of the men's secretary to the Sectional Board, which the Report recommends, does not in any way imply recognition of the union. It is said that an official of the union who is not 'a railway employe may be selected. Of course he may. So may a lawyer, or any outside person the men think fit, be elected to the position. But this secretary, even if he be the official of the union, is not elected as a representative of the union. He is not even elected by the union men, but by the railway servants, , union and non-union alike, who may happen to constitute the Sectional Board. To attempt to convey the impression that this recommendation of the Report is "recogni- tion in a modified form" is simply an assumption for which there is no foundation whatever. Not only does the Report not recommend recognition of the union, but in language as plain as the Commissioners dare use it says that recognition should not be given. "We think," the Report says, "that with their great responsibilities the com- panies cannot and should not be expected to permit any intervention betw,ien them and their men on the subjects of discipline and management." The significance of that paragraph is more evident in its spirit than in its words. The union does not want to interfere in matters which do not affect the men, but the union has a right to protect its members against unfair treatment in the name of discipline and management. SOME PIOUS OPINIONS.

There are a few piously expressed opinions about the possibility of good relations between the companies and the men's repre- sentatives being a good thing, and the opinion is also expressed that if that were done" in some matters and on some occa- sions "it might be helpful to both parties. But that is no recommendation of recogni- tion. In view of the fact that the North Eastern Railway Company does recognise the unions, and does treat with the union officials, all this talk about the dangers of permitting the union to interfere in matters of discipline and management seems not very far removed from nonsense. The most sur- prising thing of all about this Report is that it is signed by two trade unionists. lam sure their explanation and defence will be waited with anxiety, and heard with interest.

div.head: WHO WANT RECOGNITION?
div.p: WHO WANT RECOGNITION?

It is often pointed out that the majority of the railway workcrs are not connected with the union. That weakens the case for recognition, I am quite ready to admit, but it does not by any means destroy it. There

are something like 150,000 railway men in rthe trade unions. Is that a fact that can be 'ignored? There may be something to be sktid against the union being recognised as the representative of all the workmen, but surely a combination of 150,000 men is entitled to be heard on its own behalf. If the union cannot speak for all railway servants it can speak for its own members; it can put forward the collective plea for these men ;ancl_if.the men outside the unions . .

are quite satisfied with their conditions, the companies ought to pay some regard to the dissatisfaction of 150,000 of their servants. The unions only ask to speak for their own members. They do not claim to be recognised as the representatives of the non-union men.

div.head: GENERAL DISAPPOINTMENT.
div.p: GENERAL DISAPPOINTMENT.

The leaders of the railwaymen have expressed their bitter disappointment with the recommendations of the Report. They complain not only of the absence of a recom- mendation of recognition, but of the recom- mendations in regard to the procedure under the Boards. On that matter I have no qualifications to speak, but it is clear that there are all the possibilities of very serious trouble in the present situation. I do not suppose I have any influence with railway- men, but if I had I should urge them not to allow their natural chagrin and disappoint- ment to drive them into rash action. The situation is extremely difficult, and it will require the greatest skill. to steer safely through it. But whether the difficulties can be overcome by peaceful negotiations or not, I do hope that the men will not prejudice a good ease by any ill-considered and precipi- tate conduct. They have the sympathy of the public on their side in their demands for improved conditions, and if they act with calmness, but with resolution and judgment, they will yet gain their points.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY ACTION.
div.p: PARLIAMENTARY ACTION.

An early opportunity will no doubt be afforded for the discussion of the Report in Parliament. That may help to throw some light on points which are at present obscure, among these being the unnecessary and offensive imputation that in the recent rail- way strike there was coercion and intimida- tion practised towards those who were willing to continue to work. The Report in all respects is one which might have been drawn up by the Chambers of Commerce who are now petitioning Parliament to take away the right to picket.

PELORUS JACK. A FAMOUS FISH.

I have just received an interesting letter from Mr. Fred Stott, formerly aCouncillor of our town (now of New Zealand), who read what I had to say about the famous dolphin known as "Jack. This is the letter: Grafton-road, Roseneath, Wellington, New Zealand. September 15th, 1911. "Uncle Caleb"

- Dear Sir,—ln your "Children's Corner" some months ago you made reference to " Peorous Jack" of Marlborough Sounds, New Zealand and your contemporary "Old Journalist" was good enough to correct (?) you in reference to this fish? However, "Old Journalist" was wrong for " Jack " is still alive.

' It was rumoured that the dolphin was dead, for a dead body of a similar " fish " was found on the beach in the Sounds and in all probability this was the foundation which "Old Journalist's" assertion was based on. I am sending you a press cutting regarding " Jack " which may interest you.—Sincerely yours,
FRED STOTT.

- - The newspaper cutting contains an account of "Jack" told by Kipa Hemi Whiro (there's a fine name for you) one of the Maori natives. This gentleman declared that the fish was 275 years old and had been known to his ancestors for all that period. Says Mr. Kipa Hemi Whim "We call him IKaikai-a- ware. In the ancient days Kaikai- a-waro was revered by my people, and when they went out to fish for a hapuka and rock-cod and their sea-god appeared they were always careful to throw him some of the fish as an offering—food for their taniwha and pilot. And K aikai-a- ware ' was a guide to conduct towards their destination canoes passing botween Hoiere mouth and Te Aumiti and Whakatu (where Nelson now stands). He used to precede the canoes, leading them safely along the way they were to go; and he played around their bows just as he does to-day around the steamers and the launches of the pakeha." Kipa declares that generations ago" Jack" safely guided the canoe of the tribe's chief through perilous seas. " From that day to this," the old Maori continued, " Kaikai-a- ware has been the guardian taniwha of our people, the Ngati-Kuia, when they go out upon the sea. When the white man's religion was brought to this country the fish disappeared for a time. The Maori tohungas used to repeat karakia to him, but the influence of the Christian missionaries was superior to the mana of the Maori priests. Still the priests karakia'd that he might return and be a pilot as before for the canoes

of the Maori chiefs. And in the course of after-years, when fishing was carried on in these waters, this fish reappeared. When the European and Maori fisherman cleaned their fish the remains were thrown into the sea, and were carried by the tide to the place where Kaikai-a-waro dwelt. Then he came forth, attracted by the remains of the fish floating on the waters, and it was then that he began to follow the boats of the fisher men. Then, after this there came the steamers, and the crews of those steamers threw meat over to feed him. This is why he first came out in search of passing steamers, a habit which he has continued up to the present time, when he is seen by us all on the steamers passing between Welling- ton and Nelson. Friend, I know of the reports of these days concerning the doings of this pilot-fish. I have seen him in this sound, Hoiere ; and, should any persons be ignorant of the fact that this fish was seen when the mouth of Pelorus Sound was reached, let me tell him that he was seen there by my forefathers. It was my tribe who were the rangatiras that owned this fish, down from my ancestors to me and my people."

THE PLAGUES IN CHESHIRE.
A MINGLED RECORD.

In recent articles we have touched one of the most terrible chapters in human history, the great plague of the seventeenth century. It is a subject one would gladly miss save that the dark narrative throws into such bright relief the heroism that always slumbers in the human heart and leaps forth in the hour of disaster..

The great plagues which devastated Europe in the Middle Ages swept over England and have left traces in local annals, and of the terrible visitation in the middle of the seventeenth century we have many traces. Despite the saddening nature of the task we propose to describe some of the grim memorials that are spread over Cheshire which belong to the dark days of pestilence.

div.head: TTHE BLACK DEATH.
div.p: TTHE BLACK DEATH.

Earliest among the great plagues of which we have any considerable record is that known as the Black Death, which during the years 1348 to 1350 destroyed a quarter of the population of Europe. As early as the sixth century the plague had done havoc through the Ronian Empire. Its symptoms were those of a malignant fever with rapid swell- ing of the glands of the body, but the disease known as the Black Death had the added symptom of black spots or tumors. Beginning in China it spread westward to Ireland, claiming in China alone 13 millions of
GRAVE STONES OF PLAGUE VI The small grave stones have since wall seen in ti

victims. In London a hundred thousand are computed to have perished and Smithfield became a large cemetery to receive their bodies. For two full years from 1348 to 1350 it spread destruction through England and it is said that half the population perished. In the absence of any carefully-made record it is difficult for the historian to test the accuracy of these statements, but it should be said that where facts are ascertain- , able they go to confirm them. Thus in the I quiet parishes of Cheshire, far removed from the cities and plague centres, during the year 1349 nearly half the clergy died. In the manor of Bucklow in 1350 the land was described as being idle and the tenants who survived had rent remitted because "there was no one to buy the produce."
Icrims IN A FIELD AT EYAM. been surrounded by the protecting ,he photograph.

opened outside the city walls and the con- tents aired. Dogs were not allowed to rove, but were to be kept in the houses. Pig keeping was restricted, and dung and filth were not to be cast within the city limits. After a generation of comparative immunity the month of September 1603 again saw Chester panic stricken. Seven people died suddenly in a house in St. John's- lane with all the symptoms of the plague. People died at the rate of sixty a week, and sufferers were isolated by being placed in wood huts built near the waterside.

In this same year Macclesfield, Congleton and Nantwich felt the plague which ran at the latter place for six months and carried away more than 400 inhabitants. It was shown that the disease had been carried Ifrom Chester.
In 1608 and again in 1610 the plague broke out and several times the Assizes were held at Tarvin and Nantwich.
After another generation of guiesence the plague broke forth in fury on June 22nd,1647 and carried away in nine months 2,100 inhabitants and this was followed by another outbreak in 1654.

The country side around Chester has thousands of unmarked graves for the dead were seldom interred in the churchyards ' probably from a fear that contagion might reach the worshippers. Only one marked field-grave exists as far as we know and this is at Lindon Common. It bears the initials E.S. and the date 1665, the Church Register explaining that E. Stonaw was buried near her own house. "She being suspected to dye of the plague. Shee but coming home the day before."
CONGLETON FINDS A FLORENCE NIGHTINGALE.

For two years Congleton was in the grip of the plague. The infection came in 1641 being conveyed in a box of clothes from London. The town tried to isolate the sufferers and erected cabins outside the town. It was then that the sad emergency produced a Korence Nightingale. Her name is familiarly given as" Little Bess" and the brave little woman stood at her post as nurse and comforter all through the awful two years of panic and pestilence. A.M.
To be Continveei.

div.head: PLAGUE IN THE CITY OF _CHESTER..
div.p: THE PLAGUE IN THE CITY OF _CHESTER..

Chester seems to have had a share of the plague from its earliest appearances right on until its final disappearance in 1666. Thus in 1507 it was visited by the "sweating sickness" which carried away 91 householders. The so-called sweating sick- ness was a fatal epidemic which ravaged Europe and especially England in the 15th and 16th centuries. Appearing first in London in 1485 it quickly spread along the lines of commerce and ran through Europe. In its symptoms it was a violent inflammatory fever which prostrated as by a blow and suffused the body in fetid perspira- tion. A violent tempest which swept England seemed to carry away the disease ' but it re-appeared in 1508 and again in 1517. Its last appearance was in Shrewsbury in 1551. The outbreak in 1517 caused much devastation in Chester and at the Cross in the centre of the city we are told" the grass did grow a foot high." Swift and fatal was the stroke of the plague. Some died while playing with their children at the street doors and at most only an hour or two elapsed before death claimed the victims. Said Dr. Caius who lived through the visitation and wrote "a boke against the sweting sickness" "At the longest to them that merrily dined it gave a sorrowful supper."

That a copy of this resolution be forwarded to his Majesty's Government, accompanied by an expression of hope that they will give facilities for this Bill." lie said that the main principle of the Daylight Saving Bill was to place • greater number f hours of daylight at the disposal of everyone, and that was obtained by simply moving tbe hands of the clock one hour forward on the third Sunday in April, and one hour backward on tbe third Sunday in September. That arrangement needed no decisive alterations in public life. Inland railway time tables would not be altered, hourx of work in I manufactories and meal times would all remain as they I were. The only difference would be that all who worked with their minds or their hands would enjoy an hour more sunlight daily, after their work was done. For all adult workpeople the advance of the hoar meant an hour's greater freshness in the morning and an extra hour's light in the evening for recreation and the oecepations or family life. plague again breaking out, and in 1574 a further alarm caused the Mayor and Alder- men to issue some regulations for the inhabi- tants. They may be studied with some advantage and with a certain melancholy interest. All infected houses were to be marked and surrounded by a wooden fence or palisade; they were to be inscribed "Lord have mercy upon us," and none of those within were to be allowed to walk forth except by licence of the Alderman of the Ward. When allowed in the streets they were to carry in their hands a token that they were infected. They must not leave home in the night,and lest they should do ao a night watch was set. Merchandise coming into the city must be

cried Lotta haefili,•ivifis a WM or the hew. "But you are always doing something of the sort to insult me. Considering that this is almost my own house, I think it is disgrace- ful, especially before a stranger." "Come, Helen, we'll go to my mother. I am sorry, Lotta;" and he drew Helen to one side. Lotta ostentatiously held her skirts aside for them to pass. "I'll save you one trouble, at any rate, Bulmer," she said as they went on. "I'll tell the woman you've jilted-Mrs. Caulfield;" and with a rasping laugh she ran downstairs.

"What does she mean, Bulmer aoked Helen in some dismay. "We never stop to ask what Lotta means. It is always enough for her if she can find something unpleasant to say. I'm sorry to say that her chief pleasure is to make other people uncomfortable." "But about the 'woman you have jilted,' I meant'

"Oh, that's an old story. My people wished me to marry Mrs. Caulfield, a little American widow with heaps and heaps of money. You saw her in the hall when you arrived. But I never meant it. Lotta thought it would be an unpleasant thing to say at the moment; and that's all about it." With that they went into Lady Trevellock's room; and when she heard the result of the interview with Sir Gregory she drew Helen to her and kissed her very tenderly. "I am very glad, my dear, very glad, indeed. I was afraid he would not consent at all. I am very proud of my dear boy, and shall be as proud of his wife. I am sure of that. I read your heart the moment I saw you; and I am sure you will make Bulmer happy. You know that we old people think so much more of money than you young ones, so you must not be surprised that Sir Gregory makes it a condition that there should be a little time."
"I am not surprised; I think I am too dazed to have any feeling but delight at the way you have all received me. Sir Gregory was kindness itself."

"I knew what the result would be when he once saw you," declared Bulmer proudly. "Of course you did," laughed his mother; and Helen blushed. "And I think I should have been just as confident in your place. And now the next thing will be to settle down to think out a plan to make the delay as short as possible. You know, Helen, this lover of your. has never had to earn a penny piece in his life; and a great many pennies will be needed."
"Oh, I shall soon find a way. If Helen can earn her own living in the plucky way the has had to, I need not be afraid." - .
"Tell me wl;ai- you do, cbild," said Lady Trevellock.

"I try to combine two things. lam a typist, and get quite a lot of work, enough to keep me very busy in the daytime; and in the evenings I get engagements to play the piano at dances, or accompanying lingers at concerts. You know that in the States it is thought to be no disgrace for a girl to earn her own living. And I like my work and am proud of my independence." "And have a right to be so, child, of course." "If it had not been for the concert work I should never have seen Helen," put in Bul- mar. "It was at a concert at a bazaar where she was playing the accompaniments that we first met, mother." "And do you sing, dear?" "A little; but " not well enough to earn money by it." "I am not altogether sorry for that, per- haps; but you shall sing to ;re while you are at the Chase;" an in this way they chatted on; and Lady Trevellock had just told Bulmer to take Helen out into the grounds, when Mrs. Caulfield came in.

"Lotta told me I should find you both hero with your mother, Mr. Trevelloek, and I thought I should like to make haste and con- gratulate you," she said pleasantly. "You will believe me, won't you, if I say that I do really congratulate you both with all my heart. I should like to be your friend, Miss Paxton," and she held out her hand, which Helen took.
"It is very good of you, Mrs. Caulfield," said Bulmer.

"I have so few friends that I shall cer- tainly welcome your friendship," said Helen quietly. But she remembered Lotta's words, and felt instinctively that there would be little real friendship between them. "Bulmer is going to show Helen the grounds, Beth," said Lady Trevellock ; and with this the two lovers went away. "Well, what do you think of her?" asked Mrs. Caulfield, when they had gone. "I think she is a sweet, lovable girl, Beth; but—" she sighed heavily, and. added after a pause. "If only there was not this horrible money trouble." "Do you know what Lotta told her?" Lady Trevellock frowned. "I hope it was nothing unpleasant." "I'm afraid it was," replied her friend, with a shrug of the shoulders. "She referred to me as the woman Bulmer had jilted. She told me so herself just now." "You did the right thing, dear, to come here at once. I cannot understand Lotta." "Nor anyone else. It made it very awk- ward. I could see that it was rankling in Miss Paxten's mind when I spoke to her. And has Sir Gregory really given his con- sent? I suppose she has no money?" "None except the little she earns. She is a brave, clever, dear child; but that will not keep her. Ido wish it could have been otherwise, Beth." "I know you do, dear. And so do I; but we must make the best of it. I declare I should like to give them some of my dollars; but as that is impossible, I must atm if I can- not help in some other way. I may be able to interest someone in Bulmer and help him on to the get-rich-quick road." . .
"You are. very god, Beth, to take it like this. But I know that in your heart you feel it keenly."

"I won't pretend to you that I don't; but there, I can't alter things; and it is my philo- sophy to make the best of matters." She shrugged her shoulders again, and then sighed heavily. Lady Trevelloek took her hand and drew her down and kissed her. "You are very brave, Beth; but I know."

"Don't, dear," and to her friend's surprise, Mrs. Caulfield bent her head and burst into a sudden passion of tears. The storm passed as suddenly as it had COMIC. She sprang up and dashed the tears from her eyes. "Oh what a fool a woman is ever to care!" she cried, and before Lady Trevellock could reply, she rushed out of the room.

Late that night, when Helen and Bulmer had been with Lady Trevellock again, and she had sent them off with the assurances of her love and pleasure at the engagement, Sir Gregory, according to his custom, came to bid .her good-night. .
"You look very worried. Gregory," she said, distressed by the change in him. . - .
"I sm very troubled &boa it all, Mary." "You have done the right thing, dear. I am sure of that."

He paused and sighed, and then murmured, 'I wonder if I have,' speaking out of his thoughts rather than in reply to her. Then he taught her eyes fixed upon him questioningly, straightened himself up, and almost as if an- wering an accusation, he said firmly: "I should do it again. I could not do otherwise," and without more, kissed her and bade her good-night, saying he needed sleep. She lay some time wondering anxiously at the cause for the strange change in him. She had never seen him in such a mood as this. And Sir Gregory. instead of sleeping the sleep of which he load spoken, went down again to his study, and sat half the night buried in troubled, nervous, _remorseful thoughts over the scene with Helen and the wrOng he had done her. And when, at length, close to the, dawn, he crept upstairs to bed, he was still -seeking to justify the deed, and still undecided whether he would take courage in the morning and tell the truth and face the conseqpences. For so many years he had lived the life of an honourable, upright, straightforMard man that he shrank from the consciousness of otsme and guilt: and, tesishied under, ill,
d spent

diirclen 01 the loan he had taken upon nausea in that moment of temptation. Before he slept he had made his resolve. He would tell the truth in the morning, lv the consequences be what they might. could not endure the life of hypocrisy constant deceit which such a shameful would entail.
