div.p: CHAPTER M.

A FATEFUL CHOICE AND AN ENGAGEMENT. But greatly to his relief, Helen appeared to take the loss of her parsers much less to heart than he had feared. In reality she was so distressed by the sight of his intense agitation and apparent grief for the "acci- dent" that her first desire was to ease his mind.
"It cannot be helped, Sir Gregory," she said, forcing a smile. "Please do not let it cause you such trotible."

110 Made a great effort to rally his self- command. "You will forgive me?' he asked. "I cannot forgive myself, however," and he held out his hand. will try to be al- ways your friend," he murmured, as Helen placed her hand in his. . .
"To have gained such a friend for more than outweighs the loss," she replied, with another smile. "I was afraid, indeed, that what I had to tell you might have had a very different result."

"I shall always be your friend," he said again, nervously. "I —I did not read the paper, but I saw the photograph." "It was what I told you—the marriage certificate of my mother to Gregory Powell and the likeness of my father." "Yes, yes. I understood that. You have another likeness, no _doubt?" _ _
"Unfortunately I have not; and of course I never knew him. My mother scarcely ever spoke of him; but I ought to tell you he was anything but a good man."

"You should not be blamed for that, my dear child," he said—ho was regaining his self-possession now and mastering his agita- tion— and it will make no difference with me. Anyone can see that you have a pure, good heart." "My mother was one of the best women who ever lived," replied Helen, "and I was brought up by her sister, as sweet and dear a woman as ever cared for a motherless child. I felt her death as keenly as if she had been my own mother."

"Poor child," murmured Sir Gregory, sympathetically. "I do not seek to know any more, my dear, but I am going to ask a Mlle favour. I would not for the world have my dear wife know of the illness which led to this accident, and, if it is spoken of, there may be questions asked which would force me to tell of it. Will you help one to keep This a secret between us two by not speaking of the papers at al?"

"Of -course I will," was the ready reply. "I will not tell even Bulmer. But of course should know my real name." .7 "Leave me to tell him that, and all that is necessary. I may find it best to tell him what has happened to-day; but there is no hurry for that. If I know your innocent secret it will be enough for the present." In this way the matter was settled, and Sir Gregory felt that he would have time in which to think what was best to be done. "Now let us speak of Bulmer," he said, after a pause. "Ilis happiness is everything to both his mother and myself, and it is for you two to think whether a life of straight- ened means, very straightened indeed, 'Will be the best for you. You young people look at these things very differently from us older ones; and Balmer has never yet felt what it i.s.to live without plenty of money."
"I am not afraid of the prospect," said Helen, smiling. "But then I have never known what it meins to have more money than just supplies the day's wants." "-'

-- "If my boy's happiness is set on a mar- riage with you, there will not be any oppo- sition from u,. You have already won your way to my dear wife's heart, and that is a long way on the road to victory." Helen's eyes brightened, and a Bush of pleasure spread over her face. "I do not think Bulmer will be afraid of the future," she said in a low voice. lie caught at her last word. "It must be the future, of course," he said slowly. "Worldly considerations must be heeded. I will speak to Balmer presently. I think he could not have a wife who would make him happier than you would, if only there were not this question of money. fie will have to make some position for himself by hard work before that future can be realised; and meanwhile you must both have patience to wait."

Helen seized his hand impulsively. "Of course we will wait, sir, as long as you wish. And I cannot tell you how deeply I feel all you have said about me. I came here with such fear in nay heart that you would have nothing to say to me. I scarcely know what I dreaded, indeed; but you have given me such hope that my heart 13 full. You are all to kind and good that—" The words failed her then, and the tears sprang to her eyes choking her utterance. "I will send for Bulmer," said Sir Gre- gory, as ho rang the bell. "But you mast not let him see you in tears, or he will fear I have been harsh and unkind."

When Bulmer came Helen was smiling through her tears, and an answering smile leapt to his eyes as they met hers. "You sent for me, sir?" he asked. "Helen and I have had a long talk to- gether, Balmer. I have told her the fact that you have no fortune of your own, and that the Chase and everything will be Lotta's at my death. She is like you in thinking little or nothing of any such matters, and I have said that if, after a lapse of time you both desire to marry, I shall not raise any ob- stacle. But you must first make a position of some sort which will enable you to main- tain yourself." Bulmer's face was full of confidence. "I ask no more than that, father," he said in- stantly. "And you, Helen?'
- • She gave no answer in words, but slipped her hand into his.

"I am auswered," said Sir Gregory. "That is a compact; and now go and tell your mother, for I think /he is just as anxious as you two yourselves." They went out together, and close to Lady Trevellock's rooms Lotta met them. With a half contemptuous glance at Helen, she turned to Bulmer.

"Well, is the important conference over/ Have I to offer my cm!gratulations?" Bulmer felt the implied sneer, and flushed with vexation. "We are going to my mother's rooms, Lotta. You may certainly congratulate us if you wish." "I am sure the family will be honoured." Helen was astonished by both the tone and the words. Elba had not done or said any- thing to account for Lotta's unpleasantness. " You will know my sister better later, , Helen said Bulmera quickly. f I ftb. woo. to snotorise f"r me,"

div.head: GREAT WHITE PLAGUE.
div.p: THE GREAT WHITE PLAGUE.
eROFR DELEPINE ON THE CAUSES AND PREVENTION OF CONSUMPTION.
Danger of Tuberculous Milk.

The campaign whi,h the Warrington health authorities are waging against the great white plague—consumption—shoukl receive an impetus from the interesting and valuable lecture given in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening by Professor Delepine, of Manchester. The large audience was indicative of a great awakening of public interest in the question, and credit is due to the Warrington °Risers Guild of Help for affording this opportunity of enlightenment upon the causes of the disease and the precautions ts be taken against it. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Jo, eph) presided and amongst others present were : Alderman James Evans (chairman of the Health Committee', Dr, J. Cools Hibbert (medical officer of health), the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) Revs W. 13racecamp, J. Davies and J. H. Betties, Mr. C. E Parker, Captain G.ll Crotfield, Mr. R. S. Towuroe, Mr. J. A Itansoroe and Mr. Wilfrid J. Rowland (secretary of the Guild.) The Al ...NOR introduced Professor Delepine as ore of that band of distinguished men to whom we would have to look still farther in the future for the prevention of disease and the arresting of the extermination of the hest of our race. Ccnsumption was probstily

TIIE GREATEST ENEMY KNOWN TO TIM. HUMAN RACE in the way of disease. It was estimated to be respons- ible for one death out of every ten, and that was a very modest computation, some authorities putting the proportion at one in seven. On either estimate, con- sumption was evidently the chief messenger of death to mankind and it therefore behoved us to do what we could to prevent the spread of such a dire malady. In that work everyone c mid take a share. The bacilli which gave rise to consumption were obtained from various sources, chiefly from patients who had already contracted the disease. Milk was another cause and he should put meat last. As far as his knowledge went, meat had not been clearly. proved to he a direct cause of tubercle. Even supposing that there were germs in the meat, it was generally sterilised by cooking and therefore was not anything like so dangerous as some other causes. Milk might be looked upon as a medium cause, contamination being much more probable in the case of cows with tuberculous udders. The danger did not exist in the milk itself except through the mixture of tuberculous matter during the process of extracting the milk from the udder. Transmission of the germs from patient to patient was an alarmingly fruitful cause of consumption. When they considered that one or Lao billions of bacilli could be given off by an advanced patient in twenty-four hours, they realised the danger which accrued from those bacilli getting into the air and being inhaled by other people. The sputum from a consumptive person should be most carefully guarded and treated. One person out of every sixty, at the lowest estimate, was infected with consumption. At a conference which he recently attended, one of the speakers created mingled consternation and amusement by saying he believed that three out of every five persons in the room had been or were actually suffering from consumption. (Laughter). One way of conquer- ing diseste, continued the Mayor, was

I TO LESSEN DESTITUTION, Disease meant a great financial loss to the community and health was a precious asset. Consumption was a chronic disease—whether it terminated in recovery or death, it extended over twelve or eighteen months—and therefore the monetary loss was much greater thin in the case of an acute disease like pneumon.a, which terminated in a week or two. In Warrington the Health Committee, under the guidance and advice of the Medical Officer, had been doing a good work in preventing the spread of the malady. Wariington had what protably no other tows of its size possessed—a sanatorium of its own. The institution was small, but It was the beginning, they hoped, of a great effort. They had also a number of lady health visitors who were doing an educational work in telling patients how they should conduct themselves so as to be as little danger as possible to those around them. In conclusion, the Mayor expressed the indebtedness of the Health Committee to the Guild of Help, for its co-operation, (Applause). PROFESSOR DELEPINE'S LECrURE.

Professor DELEPINE said the interesting ceremony which took place at Sankey last August must have impressed all the citizens of Warrington with the importance of the subject upon tibia he bad to speak. The Mayor, when opening the Sanatorium, said very I justly that the most important thing was to try to prevent the syread of consumption and Dr. Hibbert pointed out the necessity of dealing with advanced I oases of the disease, and more especially with patieota I whose surroundings were favourable to the spread of infection. That was a doctrine which he (the Professor) bad preached for a great many sears, and he need hardly any how delighted he was when be heard that the Warrington Health Committee was giving to other , authorities

div.head: AN IMPORTANT LEAD
div.p: AN IMPORTANT LEAD

.„.. in that matter. He did not came therefore, to break new ground but to make them realize how much they could help the excellent work of their authority by their own efforts. According to the 72nd annual report of the Registrar General, the mortality from tuberculosis continued to decrease and was lower in 1909 than in any previous roar. The deaths assigned to tuberculous affectiona in the aggregate numbered 54,425 Tuberculosis was responsible for 10•5 per cent. of the mortality from all CAWS, and foes death rate of 1,523 per million living at all ages and of both maim. " Lot us consider" continued the Professor what a mortality of 54,425 means. It means that during the year 1909 there were killed by tuberculosis every day 150 persons in England and Wales. Imagine a series of railway accidents., shipwreck., explosions, wars, dro., causing 150 DEATHS DAILY

for a whole year, and think of the consternation such a state of things would cause. But we are told that the mortality during 1909 wai lower than in any previous year, end if we look at the statistics for previous periods we find that 50 years ego the rate of mortality from tuberculosis was more than dcuble what it is at present. Since 1867 there has been a gradual and steady reduction in the number of deaths from tuberculosis, including consumption. It is worthy of notice that it I was in 1865 and 1866 that Villemin announced that tuberculosis was a contagious, and therefore preventable disease. Previous to this, consumption was supposed to be an hereditary disease which could not be prevented by ordinary sanitary measures. If no Improvement had taken pities between those days and now, more than 300 people would be killed daily by the white pl foe in England and Wales at the present day. Is this stupendous amount of suffering and loss of life necessaiy ? Certainly not, since we have already been able to reduce it by one-half in fifty years. (Applause.) Is it necessary to wait another fifty years to bring the number of daily casualties to 73? No, it is not neces- sary to wait FO long ; in fact,there is no reason wby the white plague should not

- RAPIDLY BECOME AS EXTINCT in this country as leprosy, typhus, hospital gangrene and many other plagues. (Applause.) We know tat the ditease is caused by a germ, we know where it is found, how it gets into our body, what it does when it is there. We know also that by taking certain simple precautions we can tight these germs successfully. If all this has been proved, why is it that ' tuberculosis is still going on? The only possible answer to this question is that there are not many who really believe that the teachings of science are based on actual facts. This disbelief is in great part due to the smallness of the germ of consumption which renders it invisible to the ordinary eye." Continuing, the pro- fessor said it was about 29 years since the late Pro- fessor Koch discovered that the cause of consumption wns a minute fungus which be called the bacillus of tuberculosis. This bacillus was so small that it could be sees only with the help of a powerful microscope. it was undoubtedly a living being, for it multiplied fairly rapidly in the tissues of ita victims. It could also be made to grow outside the body, but fortunately for us, it did not grow readily at the ordinary temperature of the air. A single bacillus was a little cell invisible to the naked eye, but after dividing over and over again. the cell gave rise to masses which were quite visible. Those masses or colonies were made up of millions of bscilli. In that way it was possible for many gallons of milk or several pounds of dust to be infected without there being anything to show, on ordinary examination, that the milk or the dust was capable of causing tutereulosis. Let them suppose that a consumptive person had been spitting indiscriminately on the floor of a room, and that the spit had been allowed to dry on the floor. The spit of such a 'talent was full of tubercle bacilli, and sr hen it was dry it crumbled into dust, which might he raised by draughts or when the floor was swept by a broom or a skirt. If, while the room was full of that dust, s person happened to breathe the dusty air, some of the dust would pass into the windpipe and might even reach the lungs. Much of the dust we breathed never reached the lungs, it was stepped in the nese, windpipe and 'dirge air passages and was expelled again from the body or passed into the alimentary canal. When the air parolees and the lungs were already dieeased, the tubercle Lotrilli ()Wined a foothold more easily. The professor next referred to the light which went on between tutercle bacilli and the minute cells

in the body. Sometimes the baccilli were stronger than the cells, sometimes the cells were stronger than the bacilli, the latter being generally the case when the cells balonget to a healthy, strong body and had not been weakened by starvation, fatigue, excesses or disease. A large number of persme were exposed to tuberculosis infection at some time or other during life and had resisted it successfully. In other cases unfortunately the bacilli spread, killed more and more cells, and the dead tissues ultimately broke down and were expectorated, large cavities being produced in that way. It was when that stage had been reached that consumptive patients formerly consulted doctors. It was then

TOO LATE TO REPA IR Tli E MISCIIIr.O already done, and the patients hal reached that stage when they became danger to their neighbours. The disease could fortunately be dealt with it an earlier stage at the present day. (Hear, hsar ) The Professor then outlined the developmeht of the disease in the various organs of the body, resulting in scrofula, ulcera- tion Ste. Tuberculosis dust, caused by the spit of con- sumptives, was one of the chief sources of tuberculosis in man, in cattle, and in some of our pots, snob as dogs and cats. When

ABSOLUTE CLEANLINESS was observed and the fl sore, walls, furniture and hang- ings were kept free from organic accumulations, that source of danger was considerably reduced. But patients in a state of advanced tuberculosis were always a source of danger, unless they were careful to dispose of their discharges in such a way as ts prevent contamination of their surroundings and to make it possible to disinfect those infectious products thoroughly. The danger of consuming tuberculous milk was certain and hal been proved by the actual occurrence of tuberculosis in children who had been fed on milk from tuberculous cows. Experiments on young animals such as kittens, rabbits, pigs and calves had shoan that it was quite easy to produca tuberculosis by feeding them on moderate quantities of tuberculours milk or other tuberculous products—a single feeding on tuberculous milk was sometimes enough. The step taken eighteen months sacs by the Warrington Health Committee to

PREVENT THE BALE OF TUBERCULOUS MILK in the town SINI9, therefore, one of great import:hoe, and he was glxd to find the: the quantity of tuberculous milk distribated in Warrington had c3nsiderably diminished during that period. From April 1910 to September 190 31 sa.nples were examined, and 7 were found to be tuberculow, giving a percentage of 205. From October 1510 to March 19. 1,40 :samples were examined of which only two were tub3rculoux, the percentage being 4.3. From April 1911 to September 1911 the rewilts were: 35 samples examined; two tuberculous; 57 pr cent. Diring th 3 Ilrit period 2; farms were inspe3ted and nine or 391 per cent tuberculous cows were foun I. In sibieTiont periods, whether through the action of the authority or in cat:- sequence of the farmer removing infected animals of his own free will, Um percentage fell to 7.1 and 69 showing that eighteen months work of the Health Committee had been very useful. (Applause.) Summing up the bearing which the faats he had brought before the audience had on the methods of prevention, the Professor said they had seen that

(I) Well-nourished persons resisted better than ill- fed persons, therefore,good sound feeding was desirable. The appetite was stimulated by reasonable exercise and cool, bracing air, and was reduced by cjrfl lament and heat, therefore, exercise in the open air vas desirable. (2) Excessive fatigue and excesses, more especially when asslciated oath insufficient feeding, diminished resistence to infection. It was, therefore, necessary to regulate habits, work and feeding no as to prevent the occurrence of exbaustion. _

--(3.)—Va-rio-u-s—cli-s-e-as-el. and lesions predisposed to tuberculous infection. It was thsrefore necessary to remove from the neighbourhood of the sick any possible source of infaciion, however slight. (4) Tuberculous sputa and other discharges were very infectious, whsthar in the fresh or is the dry state. Therefore, it was nesessary to sea that no accumulation of those products could occur about the person of tuberculous patients, in their houses, in public places, dio. Absolute cleanlinesu of the patient was also an essential thing. (5) Rooms or other places where consumptive patients had lived and where contamination with sputa , might have taken place, were dangerous, especially when dust was raised in them by careless sweeping, dusting or draughts. Theref ore, rooms which are or had been occupied by consumptives rendered helpless by the progress of the diva.° or who could sot have bawl taught carefulness, wars &marlin to other people. Those rooms should be thoroughly disinfected before they were used again, and should not be shared by other people while they were occupied by consumptives. (6) Overcrowding& ighich increased the chances of contact with tuberilllwbs patients esti which rendered cleansing difficult, favoured infection. Therefore, measures should be taken against overcrowning. (7) Tubercle bacilli were rapidly killed by exposure to sunlight and more slowly by diffused daylight. Therefore an abundant supply of daylight should be obteiu.o I.by all available means. ; . . .

(8) Tuberculous food, and mwo especially tuberculous milk, was an important source of infection. Therefore, every precaution should be taken to exclude tuberculous food from our markets, and as this could not be done rapidly, all food liable to tuberculous infection should be cooked or boiled E 0 as to kill tuberole bacilli. This was of special importsnce in the case of cows' milk. Cases of advanced tuberculosis, concluded the Professor, were the chief source of infection. When patients were unable through weakness, insufficient training, wont of means or accommodation, to observe the prec liltiOnS which were needed for the protection of their family and neighbours, they should be provided with adequate homes in institutions where they would be well cared for. Such homes, or HORSES OF RETIREMENT, w. uld be havens of rest for many whose life was rendered miserable by want of proper care and whose presence in crowded places was a source of danger oven to those they loved best. The patients should still be able to see their friends, but under conditions which would secure safety. Those able t, work should still be able to follow their avocations, do useful work and keep their interest in life. The provision of such houses of retreat for the benefit of those who could not take owe of themselves or be taken core of at home was

A CRYING NERD, and would be, from the preventive point of view, more useful still than sanatoria. To prevent any misconception, he wishel to mace it clear that in pleading for houses of retirement, he did not speak against sanatoria, and more especially against self- supporting sanatoria. For those who could not afford to meet the cost of treatment at home or in a sanatorium, it was obvious that institutions, entirely or partly supported by public grants and voluntary contributions, were a necessity in the same sense as hospitals and convalescent homes. It was, however, bad policy not to supply at the same time suitable places for the care of advanced oases of con- sumption who could not be cared for at their own homes, or benefit permanently by treatment, and who were the means of increasing the number of persons requiring sanatorium treatment. He was, therefore, in perfect agreement with the policy of the Warrington Health Committee in opening the institution at Sankey. (Applause). The lecture was made additionally interesting by a series of lantern slides. THE GUILD AND BEGGING IMPOSTERS. Mr. J. A. RANSOM m, in a short address on the objects; of the Guild, emphasised the fact that it was not con- nected, directly or indirectly, with any political party. It was co-operating with other agencies in the town—clergy and ministers, Guardians of the poor, public health and education departments, Labour Exchange, police and N.S.P.C.C.—in a great effort to help those in poverty and distress by means of personal service. The Guild had now BM organized voluntary helpers. (Applause.) As choosing the necessity for an organization which could impartially sift all applica, lions for assistance, Mr. Rees une said tint when investigations were made, it was often found that a case was very similar to one which had cropped up in another ward under another name. People moved about from one address to anottur, changing their names and sponging on the good-hearted community, and it was part of the Guild's business to prevent such !rands. (Applause.) Ile implored the audience to cease assist- ing the promiscuous beggar. If charitably-disposed people would put into the funds of the Guild money which they gave away to beggars—most of whom were scamps—they would be doing much more good with it. (Hear, hear.) The Guild was an excellent training school for social work, as its members secured a first- hand acquaintance with the troubles which existed amongst the poor. (Applause).

COMPENSATING THE FARMER. Alderman JAMES EVANS proposed a vote of thanks to Professor Delepine. He said that however energetic local autheritiee might be in dealing with the question of tuberculous milk, there were difficulties which at present lay beyond their power to remody. If on inspection of a herd, a cow was found to be infected, they could only demand its isolation. It then became possible for the farmer to sell the cow to a dealer who would take it into 110,116 other county and dispose of it, with the result that another toes received the contaminated milk. Local authorities regarded that as a serious grievance. ((fear, hear.) Some of them thought, rightly or wrongly, that the question would soon have to los

TRIATED ON NATIONAL LINE, (Applause.) It was for the nation's good, and no local authority could find the finance to deal effectively with the difficulty. The funds ought, therefore, to come out of the Imperial Exchequer. When a cow was found to be tuberculous, the local authority should have power to ray that it should not leave the premises except for the purpose of being slaughtered. Although infected milk was no largely responsible for deaths from con- sumption, the Board of Agriculture and the Board of Trade were at present content to look on. Nothieg that the local authorities said could impress them with the importance of taking immediate remedial measurer. Why Rectos. it became a question of money. They could not expect that the farming interest, through no fault of their own, should be called upon to bear the lose of the animals that had to be slaughtered. S)me provision would have to be made not only for the son- (location of tuberculous meat but for
cOMPRN:ATION. Ile was glad to say that in Warrington he binchers displasod a willingness to co-nparate with the Health Committee. Many tit them restlily acquainted the

inspectors with any suspicions conditions that might be found in the slaughter houses. The Health Com- mittee wanted people to begin to think about these questions for themselves. The objeot of the sanatorium at Sankey was two-fold. In the first pile° they intended to educate one section of patient woo on their recovery would be able to go home and acquaint 1 their friends with the proper methods of treatment. They also hoped to take petients away from poorer houses, where there was no convenience or isolation, and thus protect the other dwellers in those houses (Applause.) The I{3V. W. BRACECANtr, in seconding, said the only regrettable feature was that the very people they wanted to reach were not present at the lecture. It therefore, behoved members of the Guild to spread the valuable information which Professor Delepine had given them. The greatest hindrance GO 113CMI reform was ignorance. Many things were being done in War- rington to improve Ile liven of the people. Ile regarded the baby chow as a grand move and the regular instruction to mothers on the feeding of infants must also do a wonderful amount (A good. Ile would like to urge the necessity of deaths from collars option being at once reported to the authorities, as harm might often be done if the corpse was allowed to remain too long in an over-crowded house. Many people had also failed to learn the foolishness, from a health standpoint, of sleeping with their bedroom windoas closed, 'the vote was heartily posted. The RECTOR proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding. Captain CROSFIELD seconded and thanked the Mayor, Aldermen Evans and the Health Corn nittee for the broadminded way in which they had welcomed and assisted the work of the Guild of Help. (Applause). The Mayor's brief *okra° slicdgmeut concluded an interesting meeting.

CONSUMPTI ON.

On Monday,under the au micas of the Warrington Guild of Help, Professor Delepine lectured on this aubject in the Co-operative Hall, ant the occasion affards4l3 an opportunity to supplement what I have previously written of it in this column. I can merely state what strikes me as the main points for the leader's mature consideration . Surely, next to cancsr. consumptio is our most terrible foe, for the deaths fro n the latter actually exceed the combined zyinotic death rate! Tne insidious dis-ase seems rather to be transmitted to those who are unfortunately ausceptible than to be in itself here Mary The nature of one's occupation may easily be a pre-disposing cause, undoubtedly, the lack of _fresh air is, and all ought to slev with bedroom windows open. Th 3 dread disease in questi no has three stages : curable, ddubtful, and hopeless. It is essentially on, as to which preventive measures are essential. Hence the present movemont far the instruetion of the public at large; obvi only, their intelligent co operation is necessary if the ravages of the " white plague " are to be effectually stayed—and, otherwise, how serious would be the refl-ction upon our civilisaion, our humanity, and even our presuored instinct of eel!- preservation. In a former reference I mentioned that, my sister-in-law being matr ,n at a sanatorium, I had fully availed myself of the chance to study at first hand the effiaacy of the treatment and the general useful- ness of such institutions. In the meantitn3 I have extended my observations and inquiries, visiting Manchester among other import tat centres, and my conclusion is that, although the up-to-date methods strictly followed at such places miy not as yet have proved as successful as was at the outset anticipated, the Provision of these institutions will remain a sacred duty so long as they are regarded as an indispensable adjunct. However, prevention being proverbially and emphatically better than the care which is so diffic ult and comparatively rare, it behoves those who are peculiarly liable to infection to be ever on their guard, and all alike to do what in them lies to support the enlightened reformers now at work in oar midst in such efforts as lest Monday night's lecture revcaled. THE LOCAL BIBLE CENTENARY.

0.1 Thursday evening (Bible Sunday preceding), the hundredth anniversary of the Warrington Auxiliary to Cie British and Foreign Bible Society WJS formally celebrated at a largely attended meeting in the Parr Hall. It may here bs noted the the parent sociaty was founded in 1808 for the purpose of issuing the simple text of Holy Scripture in all the languages of the world. A meeting was held in the old London Tavern, in Bishopsgate-street, on March 7th of that year, and was attended by "abut three hundred respectable persons of different religious denomina- tions." Granville Sharp presided, and William Wilberforce was among the speakers. The outcome of this gathering was the formation of the Society. The first committee included the names of Zachary Macauley, Charles Grant, William Alers Hanley, and Joseph Reyner, the &SS treasurer of the Religious Tract Society. The first to hold the office of president was Lord Tynenmuth, who was Goaernor-General of India from 1792-98. For thirty years he devoted the best of his energies to the cause. This lengthy record was, however, beaten by Lord Shaftesbury, who became president in 1851, and for thirty-four years adminis- tered the affairs of the Society with extraordinary sagacity. The Earl of Harrowhy followed, and the vacancy caused by his death was filled by the Marquis of Northampton. From 1801 to 1815 the Committee of the Society met in the counting-house of Messrs. Hardcaatle and Rayner at Old Swan Stairs, but at length the Society moved to premises of its own in Earl-street, near Blackfriars Bridge. This first home of the Society was known as the Old Bible House. In the construction of Queen Victoria-street the building was demolished, and in 1866 the late King (then Prince of Wales) laid the foundation stone of the present Bible House, which was erected by the munificence of private donors. Warrington mani- fested the utmost sympathy from the first, and, as was made plain on Thursday night, early began actively to co-operate, and has throughout the intervening five score years maintained a more or less intitnate association with headquarters. DAYLIGHT SAVING.

I heartily commend the courage and the ability with which, at Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council, Alderman Pierpoint proposed his resolution in support of the Daylight Saving Bill. Why with all their red taps and antiquated methods, even the permanent officials of your Circumlocution Office have ventured to experiment in daylight saving, and have been no , encouraged as to favour more extended trials along , these tines; indeed, it is by no means improbable that the principle of Mr. Willett's pet measure may by next summer be adopted in other Government depart- ments as it already has been by the Board of Educa- tion authorities. Two or three years ago, the inhabi- tants of Nelson, British Columbia, discussed the project which which was debated in oar own Council Chamber on Tueeday, and the City Council, satisfied , that the great majority of the citizens desired the I change, issued an ordinance altering the civil time of 'the place from Pacific Standard time —Nelson is in the Pacific Standard zone —to Mountain Standard time, and thus simply delayed the time of sunset by a full hour. This very yeaar, the citizens of Cincinnati, Ohio, and time others in the United States, decided to put their clocks on one hour on May!, and keep them thus ahead of their real zone time until the first of the present month—a highly appreciated reform promoted by the National Daylight Association which came into existence in America to push Mr. Willett's idea. Since that was done, the official time of Fringe has been altered, and Belgium has been similarly agitated. True, Mr. Willett has yet to 90e his daylight saving scheme legalised in his own country; but as Mr. Winston Churchill said at the Guildhall ciemonstra- tiot. in its favour, future generations will unquestion- ably enjoy the great advantage of this system. A grat<tful posterity, dwelling in a brighter and healthier world, will raise statues in honour of Mr. Willett, and will decorate them with sunflowers on the longest day of the year. The progress of the idea during the last four years, said the Home Secretary earlier in the sone speech, had been one of continuous conquest. All attempts to deride it or langh it out of court bad faile.l Enormous mountains of prejtidiee, of apathy, of impatience, and of incredulity had been removed.

Let it be repeated that the proposal is simply that the clocks of the country should be set forward for one hour during the night of the third Sunday in April, and set back for one hour during the night of the third Sunday in September. A. hundred and fifty-four hours more daylight will be secured in effect for the whole people of these islands and to the vast mojority of these persona these 15 hours more daylight will be 154 It urn more daylight ' leisure. On the occasion to which I have referred it was stated that the principle was aupported by 46 Chambers of Commerce, by 170 city C wporations and Town Councils, by 265 members of Parli tment, by 39 trade unions and by 338 other societies, clubs and associations. Soup who do not agree with what was advanced in its favour at this week'a Council meeting Ihere may he repeating the question—" Why do you want an Act of Parliament at all ? What is there to prevent anyone who likes getting up as early. aa he chooses in the summer time ?" The answer la that it is impossible for individuals to alter their hours of business and life apart from the general move- ment of the society in which they live without great inconvenience and difficulty. As the authority whom I have freely quoted put it, if the public office or the factory advances the hours of its business in the summer time, while at the same time the general hours of the community remain unaltered, there is an immediate discordance and di-location throughout all the existing arrangements of the day. Trains, meals, amusements, bedtime—all are out of gear so far as those who have male the change are concerned. At a 'score of points they find themselves out of meta with the extraordinary time- table of the nation. The Rev. H. A. Lester, formerly of Warrington Training College, has now entered upon his duties as Director of Sunday schools in the London diocese. Anxious to enlist the sympathy and support of super. 1 intendants and teachers, Mr. Lester visited the Deanery of Willesden on Saturday, and, at St. Matthew's Church mete large body of Sunday schocl teachers from Willesden, Harrow, Edgware Hendon and other place,. He was introduced by the Rural Dean, Pre- bendary F. Wayland Joyce, Vicar of Harrow, and, in the course of his addreas.said he was desirous of coming amongst them, not as an Inspector, but as a co-opera- tive worker—that was, consulting with them as to the best methods of proniot ins efficiency in Sunday school work, for the teachers most be as efficient in religious instruction as the teacher in the day schools was in Imparting secular knowledge. - - - - ••

Wycliffe PSI. Socelty. There was a smaller attendance than usual on Sunday. Mr Joseph Owen presided and spoke upon the greatness of the P.S.A. movement both in numbers and useful- ness. Mr Peake gave the address upon " Gambling " his text being " Let everyone seek not his own, but everyone the good of others." Gambling was wrong and bed in its effect upon others, specially upon the young life in the offices and works of the country. Something ought to be done to prevent the madness of gambling getting bold of our young life. Miss Elsie Hewitt sang sweetly " 0 Divine Redeemer and " The Gift." Mr Payton presided at the organ. The Chairman read the lesson and the Secretary led the prayer. Two new members received a hearty welcome.

Cockhedge Mission. On Sunday, in connection with the above, the harvest festival was held. al iss V Taylor gave a very useful address to the azholars, The Rev John Yonge took the service in the afternoon and Councillor It Nenshall in the evening. There was an excellent attendance et each service. Os Monday evening the usual enter- tainment and sale of fruit, was held but owing to state of weather it was not very well attended. The committee takes this opportunity of thanking their many friends for gifts of fruit, flowers and vegetables, and the artistes for their cervices on the Monday evening. Pulpit supplies as follows :—Octoher 28th, Mr fl Syers ; November sth, Mr H New ; November l2tb, vacant • November 190, Mr W Twins; November 28th, Mr J St. John's Presbyterian Guild.

In spite of the heavy ram there was a good attend- ance at the meeting of the above society on Monday evening when an illustrated lantern lecture was given by the Rev. NV. Reid on " Wales : Her Churches and Heroes." The history of the Principality wan sheen by a large number of slides, portraying the many beactiful spots well known to touriste, the castles, churches, and centres of commercial activity, and finally dealt with the men who in spite of great perse- cution did so much for the religious freedom of the land they loved so well. In a clear and concise manner the lecturer traced the history of this movement, giving short biogrephical sketches of some of the heroes con- cerned, down to the time of the greatest of them all— Mr.Lloyd-George. Musical selections of hymns com- prised by Welshmen were given by members of the choir during the evening, and at the close a most hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, lanternist and singers for a most enjoyable programme. St. John's Presbyterian Church. " Holy Scripture and Progress" was the Sunday ' evening topic at St John's, when the Rev. W. Reid took for his text Psalm cix. 100 : " I understand more than the ancients because I keep Thy precepts." Pro- ceeding to establish a point of connection with big Tercentenary sermon of last Marcb,the preacher touched on the continued opposition offered to the placing of the Bible in the people's tongue in the people's hands, and passed on to the incident of Mary Jones and the formation of the Bible Society, and its results. The reasons for this Book becoming the people's book, said he, were that it conveyed the light of God as seen in the development of man's conception of God and of himself ; that it declared the everlasting distinctions between righteousness and evil ; that it was the charter of man's freedom and the doom of priestly pretension!, feudel laws and everything savou ring of arrogance and tyranny ; that it struck tho note of man's responsibility, and was the book of Jesus Christ and the immortal hope. Reference was made to the work under its inspiration, and the testimony borne by Lincoln, by Wilberforce and Granville Sharp, by John Howard and Elizabeth Fry; by Havelock, Gordon, Livingstone, Carlyle, Ruskin and Gladstone. Speech, said the preacher, literature, art, music, had been inspired by it, and it had crested a national conscience which WM entering into and uplifting matters social, economic and political, and if that harvest of their , fathers' sowing which they (his hearers) were reaping was to be surpassed or even rtalized for their children , it Was necessary that they should now more earnestly and extensively than they were to-day doing. Refer- ences were also made to the Revs. Alexander Hay, Joseph Wood and J. B. Johnstone, former ministers of St. John's, who had been officially connected with the local auxiliary of the Bible Society. - - -

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

RUNCORN TRADESMAN'S DEATH. The death took place on Sunday night of Mr. Samuel Coventry, one of the oldest Runcorn tradesmen. For a great many years he had a tailoring business. 115 was a well-known Wesleyan local preacher and a veteran member of the Old Folks' Treat Committee, which he helped to found. CONFESSION AFTER FIFTEEN YEARS. At Widnes, cn Monday, Annie Lythgoe (40), residing at 26, Davis-street, charged with the concealment of the birth of her child in December, 1896, under dream stances already reported, and her husband, John,charged with aiding and abetting, were committed to take their trial at the Liverpool Assizes. Bail was allowed. IN IMPUDENT FRAUD. At Runcorn, on Monday,Frederick Carey, of Runcorn, was summoned for travelling without a ticket from Lime-street to Runcorn on October 21st. He pleaded guilty Mr. G. IL Smythe, of Euston, said the offence was aggravated by C.rey's subsequent behaviour. Os October 14 be travelled from Lime-streot to Ruocorn by the 11.5 p.m. train. When he arrived at Runcorn he , found a platelayer on duty, and decided with consider able astuteness to save hie ticket for another occasion. He said " Contract," and when the platelayer asked to look at it he remarked that it was a pity the railway company did not keep men on duty who knew con- tractors. Then he walked away. On October 21 he tried to pass the barrier with the ticket for October 14 and this was the offence for which he was summoned. A previous offence of a similar character was proved in 1908, and defendant was lined 40s. and XI la lid costa, with the alternative of fourteen days' hard labour. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The hural Council was held immediately after the Board of Guardians. Mr T Wright presided, and the officers present were Messrs G F Ashton (clerk), W E Hough (assistant clerk), .1 Swinton and W Diggle (surveyors), J Farrington (inspector) and Dr Adams Adana (medical officer of health). TH IS INSURANCE BILE. The Clerk reads letter from the secretary to the Rural Council Association calling attention to clause 46 of the National Insurance Bill dealing with excessive sickness and the responsibility of the local authority thereto. The association had had the clause under discussion at their conference and a resolution was adopted for the omission of the clause. lithe Council agreed with the resolution they were asked to communicate with their member and ask him to oppose the clause when it cameoo for discussion in Committee. The Clerk said if it was held by the officer who made the inquiry that excessive sickness was due to the neglect of the local authority to enforce the Act they could put the expense upon that authority. Mr. Linaker, Ben., moved that they agree with the tenor of the resolution and they communicate with representatives for the divisions. This was agreed to.

RUNCORN BOARD OF' GUARDIANS. The Runcorn Board of Guardians were held on Tues- day afternoon in the boardroom of the Dutton Work- house. Mr. J. Spruce presided over a poor attendance, which was no doubt due to the inclement weather. The officers present were Messrs 13 F Ashton (clerk) IV E Hough (assistant clerk) W It De Prez, T Cook, F Pearson (relieving officers) and J Parsons (master). WORKHOUSE CHILDREN'S NEW HOME. The Boarding Out Committee reported having inspected Dutton Lodge with a view to considering its suitability as a home for poor children and the mob- committee who had previously been in communication with the agent of the premises reported that the premises cobld be had at the following terms :-10 years at £9O per annum and rates and taxes paid by the lessees, and there were other conditions. It was recommended to the Board that subject to certain I conditions Dutton Lodge be taken as a home for all indoor pauper children over 3 years of age except Roman Catholics, as far at the accommodation would allow, and subject to the approval of the L G 13. The Chairman moved that the report be received and adopted. They had had the matter before them time after time, and they had also had the assistance of Mr. Duff, the Local Government Board Inspector. They felt that for them to provide a home in the immediate neighboulhood for the children would be the hest course to adopt. Other systems were in vogue in other unions, but taking things all round and considering the fact that the proposed home was no near and it could be worked through the Workhouse, they felt that those proposals were the hest solution. Mr. T. Wood seconded. He thought the place was I very suitable for the purpose. It was isolated and away from the public gaze. I Mr. blawdeley : How many children will tbisaccom- , mediae ? I The Clerk : Fifty. Mr. blawdsley remarked that there were above 50 children. The Clerk said there were shoot 50 apart from the Roman Catholic children. The Local Government Board did not like there to be above 50 children in one home. Mr. Pilling remarked that if they did not have a home similar to tha one proposed they would have to build one. Under the circumstances he thought it beat to adopt the report. Fir. Hallows also supported the report. Mr. blawdaley : Is it compulsory that we should I remove the children from the Workhouse' The Clerk : Yes. I Mr. blawdsley : It might involve ninth a big thing. I am sorry that there is such a poor attendance to-day I when this important matter is being dealt with. Mr. Mclntyre remarked that there was a moral obligation in the passing of this resolution. Mr. A.R.Norrnan sold he did not think they went any further that day except to accept the offer of the owner provided they could make the building suitable at a reasonable expenditure. The recommendations were adopted. HOARD REFUSES TO ADOPT FAIR WAGE CLAUSE. The Secretary of the Runcore and District Trades and Labour Council wrote stating that his Council bad before them the newspaper report on the action of the Runcorn Guardians in retuning to adopt the fair wage clause as recommended by the Advisory Committee of Representative Governmeot departments, end the following resolution was passed : "That this Council representing 986 organised workers, regret the action taken by the Runcorn Board of Guardians refusing to adopt the fair wage clause, sal beg that the Guardians will reconsider the question," the Secretary to write to the Chairman of the Board of Guardians enclosing copy of the Fair Wage Cense approved Sty the Council. Mr. C. E. Lioaker, gen. : I move we go on to the next business. Mr. W. Mclntyre : I second. Mr. T. Wright I think wears making a mistake. Mr. Linaker : I don't. The motion was curried unanimously. TIIE LATE AIR. CONCIREFE. A letter was read from Mrs. Congreve expressing her thanks for the Board's message of sympathy and for their kindly words of appreciation of her hualoond's character. At the same time she sent in her res gelation as a member of the Ladies' Committee, which was accer ed with regret. PAUPERISM. A return as to the pauperiem for the year end:ng March 3rd, 1011, was furnished bp Mr, It. 0. Duff, the Local Government Board in.peotor, by which it was seen that the number of the paupers per 1 000 of the population in Runcorn Union was 15.46. The highest proportion in the Simi-urban Unions was at Ludlow with 2617 per 1,000 and the lowest at Tanis with 10 65. Tom were three worse and 14 better than Runcorn in the semi-urban unions. In the whole area there were nine unions better than Runcorn in this respect and 30 worse.

div.head: Penketh.
div.p: Penketh.

CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY CON, F.RT.—Tho Education Committee of the Co-operative Society of Warrington gave a concert in the Wesleyan schoolroom on Tuesday evening, Mr. S. H. Smith presiding. Evidently the people of Penketh expected a repetition of the high- class concert the society lass thename for (as the school- room was packed before the time for the concert). Nor were they disappointed, as it was up to the usual standard and thoroughly enjoyel. The artistes were Silcock (soprano), air Willett (tenor), Miss Rigby (contralto) Mr Clay (lass), and Mr W W Whittle (humorist), who was encored more than once. Miss Jarman was the accompanist. A vote of thanks was most heartily carried to the chairman and artistes and others who bad assisted in arranging such a successful evening. Wescev G CILD.—On Saturdey last the above Guild commenced their winter session by asocial held in the Wesleyan School. The Rev 11 Middlewood the presi- dent of the Guild presided, Mrs Middlewood also being present. About DO people put in an appearance which angers well for the winter session. The arrangements for the evening's enjoyment were in the capable hands of the Sccial Committee, Mr and Mrs H Ambler and Miss Moores being joint secretaries with Mr G Dale as general secretary. Songs were given by Miss D Baker,Mrs Clatworthy and Mr H Plumpton and the Penketh Tannery Prize Brass Band gave two quartettes All the items were greatly appreciated by the audience. Games were indulged in at intervals. Refreshments were handed round during the evening. An enjoyable evening was brought to a close about 10 30 p.m. by the tinging of" Auld Lang Syne." FRIENDS' SCHOOL.—In the leature hall of the above school on Monday evening, a most interesting enter- tainment was given by Mr. Thomas Rutting, late member of the celebrated Fisk University Choir (of Jubilee singers), and only surviving member of the original choir. Mr H E Brown was in the chair. Mr Rutling being a most popular entertainer it goes with- out saying that there was a crowded attendance including the pupils of the school. Mr Rutland who was a slave until he was eleven years of age, was born about 3U miles from Nashville, Tennessee, U.S.A. He divided the entertainment into three pies, English songs, plantation songs and negro melodies. During Mr Rotling's travels with the Jubilee choir he had the, honour of appearing with them before her late Nfajasty Queen victoria, and his late Alajosty,ging Edward, then Prince of Wales. Emperor William I. of Germany Crown Prince of Prussia, the late Emperor Frederick and a number of other Royaltiea.--Muster Ivor Thomas propozed, and Miss kl Woodhead seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to the lecturer and entertaiser. MR. PARKER LECTURES ON ROME.—On Wednesday evening the literary section of the Wesley Guild enjoyed a lecture, entitled " Ancient Rome," in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The lecturer vase Mr C E Parker, J.P., who has been to Rome on a visit thin year. The interesting way Mr Parker explained the different views of ancient structures that are still to ha seen after no many hundred years, proved to the audience, which was a large one despite the fact of it being such a wet night, that Mr Parker had gone to a great deal of trouble to give the members and friends of the Guild such an interesting evening. -Mr It Garnett proposed, in her usual pleasing way, a vote of thanks to the Lecturer, and Mr W E Brown, of the Friends' School (who had several of his plinths with him), seconded, and said they were very grateful to Mr Parker for his/Pry interesting lecture. Thu vote was carried unanimously. Mr I Woodward manipulated the lantern. The arrangements were carried out by the Literary Committee, of which Mr J 11 Hist') and Mr E A Murphy are joint secretaries. Lymm.

CONC.REGATTONAL CHRISTIAN SERVic E BAND.— About 30member5 assembled on Monday when the meet- ing took the form of • social, the occasion being the return of Mr. W. Thomas. Tea was pros ided. Afterwards the usual meeting was held, addresses being given by Messrs J 1-1 Molt. .1 D B Smith, and A Thomas on the subject .• Ye are my witnesses." Solos were rendered by MIMI A Miller, Mrs C Lewis, Miss E Moore, Mr G Willman, Mr .1 Hewitt, and were much appreciated. Mr. George Willan presided. Mr. Thomas thanked the members for giving him so hearty a welcome. The evening passed off in a very successful manner. Hearty thanks are due to Mr end Mrs Willan. and Misses E Sutton and F Sutton for their excellent help. Ton Lure MR. T. DIXON—The funeral of the late Mr. Thomas Dixon, of Statham, took plale at Lymm Church yard on Saturday afternoon last. The des:eased was held in the highest respect, which was clearly manifested by most of the blinds en route being drawn. Mr. Dixon was a staunch churchman and Conserva- tive. Ile had also occupied the position of teacher in the Statham Sundsy School for over 20 years. After the recent rebuilding of the Mission he was appointed a sidesmseand took a leading part in every good work. A conducted by the Rev. G. It. Thurston, who afterwards officiated at the graveside. The chief mourners were : Meows John, Thomas F Walpole, William and Roland Dixon (Ions), Mr E Davies (son-in-law), Mr John Dixon (brother), Mr John Dixon and Mr IV Walpole (nephews), Mr John Blain,Mr Parker (brothers-in-law ), Messrs. John Percival and W Denrett. Amongst others present at the graveside were Mr and Mrs S Scragg, Mrs T Appleton and Mr Moston. Wreaths were cent by the following :—"llis Loving Wife,"Jokn and Lizzie, Richard and Masie. Tom and Florence, Willie and Alice, Ernest and Bells, Mr John Dixon, Mr and Mrs W Walpole, Mr and Mrs John Cozens. Mr and Mrs W H Atherton, Mr and Mrs Walter Dennett, Mr and Ma Hankinson. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. Kirkpatrick. URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the Lvmm Urban District Council was held at the Council offices on Thursday evening, Mr 0 G Smith presiding. There were present the Rev B Thurston, Messrs T HWarberton, W G Groves, It H Gotobed. S D,vtrg, U L Welford,T Lookyer, H Holt, W Gould. W Idolised, (ohs k) D Mort (surveyor), W L Donsldson (gas manage ) and Dr de Jong (Medical officer of Health.) DITCHFIELD'S BRIDGE. At • meeting of the Roads Committee held on the 19th October the Surveyor produced an approximate estimate for new bridge amounting to £l,OOO odd, to enable an application to be made to the Road Board for • contribution. It was proposed by Mr. Davies seconded by Mr. Holt and carried unanimously, that cony of the estimate be sent to the County Council. It was proposed by Mr Groves, seconded by Mr Warburton and carried unanimously, that through a letter having been received from Mr Wiswall, engineer for the Manchester Ship Canal Company, suggesting a deputation wait upon the company to discuss the nnes- tion of a new bridge at Camsley. that Mr Davies, Mr Holt, Mr Lockyer, and the Rev hi 13 Thurston with the Surveyor be appointed the deputation to meet the Canal Company and discuss the above matter. and to obtain their views thereon and also to enqulre what amount they were prepared to contribute towards the Cog.. div.head: ---- • Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.
div.p: ---- • Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.

The League of Help Society connected with the above Misason held its annual meeting on Tuesday night, Mr George Dale, president, leing in the chair. In representing the annual report, the secretary, Mr Callum stated that the week after the last amnia) meet- ing there were eight cases on the books, -and by December 20th the number had increased to 17, all receiving help either in money or groceries. Some of these cases had been on the boors for a considerable length of time, necessitating many visits, the helper in some instances having paid as many as 20 to 30 visits to one house during the year. Without the timely prictical help of the League, some of the cases would have had to break up their homes and go into the Workhouse. The League had been able to Sad clothing, boots, blankets: &1., for several cases and two bed-rest; (which a member made and presented to the League, for the Ina of sick persons) had proved very iniefuLas also an invalid chair belonging to the mission. Some cases had teen arsistrd into regular employment and others into Canal errplo3 mint andaympathetic advice hat fleas given merely in tans-. Last Chrt,tirm they prcvidrd a good CM btmas dinner to some of the Inca nerdy men. The League had worked hand in bend with the Warrington citiz,ns Guild of Help somo of the members being connected with both organizations, which often prevented overlapping. The year was commenced in a good financial position, the balance brought forward from the previous year being £lO fis Id. The income amounted to £39 191. 91. The expenditure had bees £37 11,. 01., leaving a balance iii band of tl ds. 3d. During the evening seviiral of the helpers gave instances of the effective work of the League, and the Chairman appealed for the continued and incensed support of ell the sections of the Mission during the !coming year.

div.head: Our Lady's Latchford. Father Day and Labour Unrest.

The annual Charity Sermons in connection with Our Lady's Church, Latchford, which were held on Sunday, were rendered additionally interesting by the •isit of the Bishop cf the diocese (the Right Rey. Dr. Singleton). The special preacher was the Rey. Father Henry Day, S.J., of the holy Name, Menchester. There were good congregations at all the service., the Mayor end Mayoress (Councillor Dr. and Miss Joseph), being present in the morning, when Pontifical High Mass was celebrated by the Bishop, who was assisted by the Rev. Father .1. H. Roche (Stockport) as Master of Ceremonies and the Rev. Fathers G. Conroy and N. Doyley as Deacon and Sob-deacon respectifely. The choir ably rendered Rinck's Mars by Oyerhoffer while the " Ave Ma ia " (C. Santley), was given es • motette. The preacher in his discourre on "Prryer," gave many eloquent illustrations from the Old Testa- ment of the efficacy of prayer. He also thanked the Mayor and Mayoress for their presence. In the afternoon His Lordship administered the Sscrament of Cot.tirmatlou to upwards of G) boys and 50 girls and

In the Course of a short address the Bisholp explaired the maiming and value of that great Sacraapent and exhorted all to live up to the graces% which they were about to receive. The music, which was sweetly rendered by a choir of scholar', con- sisted of" Veni Creator" (Gregorian)" Anima Christi" (Maher) concluding with Pooch's Benediction, the " Adoremus " being by Meadelasobn. Miss F. Flood presided at the organ and contributed the following voluntaries i—Adante in 0 (F. Werdimer) "Ave Maria" (Mozart) and " Amplitre Lava Me " (Sarti). In the evenirg the service of Benediction was conducted by the Bishop. The choir sang" Magniecat " (Danb7)" 0 Salutarie" (Eiger) Litany (Tozer) " Tantem Ergo " I (Turner) "Adoremus ' (Gregorian) the service conclud- ing with the h3ran " Fnih of our Fathers" by the, whole conxregation standing. Mr. W. Wallington was I the organist at the morning and evening services. THE SOLUTION OF THE LABOUR QUESTION• Taking as the subject of his addresa at the evening service' The Labour Question," the Rev. Father Day said that the whole of the labour unrest had been brought about through the terribly unequal distribu- tion of the world's riches. There bad never been such a quantity of wealth and material as existed at the present day. The profits of capital had increased out of all proportion to the rewards paid for labour, during the decade 1E93 to 1903 the profits having risen by 20 per cent, while the wages had only increased by 10 per cent. That made it quite clear that there was a wrong distribution and that the spoil had not to' is divided according to justice. And one of the results of this was that there existed in all the civilised countries of the world, aide by side with immense wealth and luxury, extreme poverty. Another result sues the strikes which were everywhere prevalent amongst the organised industries and which led to still further poverty. Might was being tailed in to settle the question of right. Such a state of things, however, was utterly wrong and was a menace to material progress and civilizatior, commercial greed and a spirit of revolt in the ranks of labour combining to forbid a settle- ment. The strikes that were simultaneous in Austria, Spain and other countries could not be interpreted on were expressions of local discontent with Ll:reconditioner of industry. They were no such thing, but were in reality the work of the lenders of international Socialism throughout the world, who Incited social animosity and brought ebout revolution. A meeting held to encourage the new British Socialist Party culminated in a resolution expecting all Socialists in England to reject every form of zeacef el solution of the eocial question and to adopt a revolutionary policy. What was to be done? The fight would have to end and justice would have to go in between. Society was essentially an ethical organism. All its parts were subject to the moral law, which acting through the State ought to control and govern them in the interests of the whole. The solution was that the Christian frith declared what was right and insisted that right should be fulfilled. If the wages were not ad«plate, then justice declared the readjustment of binding the rich man to pay labour adequately, the worker to do his duty in return. Mr. Kerr Hardie declared at a meeting in the North of England that the Government had no power to stop strikes by means of compulsory arbitration. Could such a position be allowei ? Cer:ainly not Lin a C.riatian State where justice should prevail. The State was bound to safeguard the interests of its people and pro- tect their rights by its various powers. Just as the State had power to interfere between two individuals asserting their rights so the State must have the power to interfere between two sections or classes who were threatening to bring the whole country to ruin.

div.head: New Church.
div.p: The New Church.

The series of lectures in connection with the New Church concluded on Wednesday evening in the Masonic Hall, when the Rev. W. H. Claxton, of Kearsley, lectured on " heaven and hell: real and eternal." He said that past ideas with regard to Heaven and Hell had been mainly materialistic. They represented Heaven as being a little garden in which they would have eternal bliss and Hell as a place of eternal tire and torment. These ideas had rendered Heaven and Hell unreal to the majority of thinking men and women, causing many either to doubt the existence of a future life or to sink into agnostic or Indifferent spirits. The see doctrine was that the spiritual world was divided into Heaven and Hell but that the substantial being would he composed of a spiritual substance as this world was composed of a materiel substance. In this way would be reflected on the outward surface the inward state of goodness. Hell gas the inevitable result of the choice of evil and wos inhabited by devils and infernal spirits.

COLLIER'S DANGEROUS FOLLY.

Samuel Critchley, a daywageman. of 115, Peter- street was fined El Is. 6d or seven days at St. Helens on Monday for a breach of the Coalmines Regulation Act by opening his mate's safety lamp in the mine in I order to relight his own.

div.head: FALSE PRETENCES.
div.p: FALSE PRETENCES.

James William Worrell, of Northwich, was dealt with at St. lielens,on Saturday, charged with obtaining food and lodgings by false pretences at a house in Bicker- stuffy-street. It was stated that Worrell said he had bees engaged to erect some mschinery at Todd Bros., and he had come from Middlesborough. Mrs Kirkham the landlady, on inquiring, found that this was false, and gave him in charge. Defendant's father was present in court, but the Chief Constable said that the young man was wanted at several otter places. Ile was nineteen years of age, and WI been working for three and a half years at a boilermaker's in Northsvich, but End left and joined a theatrical company. Other offences of this description had been committed in vnrious places.—lie was sentenced to twenty-eight days' hard labour.

div.head: £l,OOO CHURCH BAZAAR.
div.p: £l,OOO CHURCH BAZAAR.

The bazaar held at St. Helens Town Hall in aid of the Sutton churches was opened on Saturday afternoon by the Mayor (Alderman Beecham). There was a large assembly, over which Alderman Dr. Bates presided. The Mayor said the bazaar had been rendered necessary by certain improvements that they desired to make at All Saints' and St. Nicholas' Churches. The Sutton parish was nothing like no rich as it used to be, owiag to residents leaving the district, but they bad done remarkably well. During the past ten months they had raised about £3OO and prepared all the articles for four of the stalls. The Vicar had appealed to outsiders for assistance. end, no doubt, would meet with a very hearty response.—The Rev. W. E. Colegrave (vicar) announced that £709 had been received on the two previous days, and he hoped that over £l,OOO would be reached before the effort closed.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
IN CASE OF INVASION. SIR JAMES BARR'S HINT TO VOLUNTARY AIDERS.

The Ashton end Newton Divisions of the Volantary Aid Detachment were inspected by Sir James Barr, the comity director, at Ashton-in-Makerfield, on Saturday afternoon. Among those present were : Lady Mary Gerard (the president), Lady Gerard, Colonel Thomas, Colonel Jackson, and Colonel Knowles of the West Lanceehire Territorial Association, Dr. and Mrs. Jackson, Die. They most be prepared to convert a country cart into an ambulance end a waggon into a hospital. In a case like that they need not he very particular whether they damned the train or not. (Laughter.) div.head: ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE ELECTIONS.
Three Contests on Wednesday Next

The Warrington municipal elections on Wednesday next seem likely to be the least interesting which have taken place for some years. There will be three contests—in Whitecross, Orford and St. John's Wards. Tuesday was the last date for the receipt of nominations and papers were handed in on behalf of the following : Ward. Retiring Councillor. Candidates. Town Hall ...Coun. Birtles Coon. Birtles (I) Whitecroas ...Coun.Hoberts Robarts (I) Mr. S. Gough (1) Ramey ...... Conn. Dickenson Coon. Dickenson (L) Orford Conn. lialliwell ...Coin. Hallivrell (L) Mr 0 F Robson (Lab) SI. John's Coun. [Ashford Coon. Laslatord (C) 111 r Jae [tampion (Soo) Fairfield Conn. Craik Conn. Craik (I) Howley Coun. Chantler Coon. Chantler (C) St Austin's... Coon. Dr. Joseph Cenn. Dr. Joseph (C) Latchford......Coun. Pemberton Coun. Pembeiton (C) Councillors Birtles, Dickenson, Craik, Chantler, Dr. Joseph and Pemberton are, therefore, returned unopposed. WHITECROSS WARD.

Mr. Henry Roberts, the retiring represen- tative, is making a vigorous fight and the ! general opinion is that he will have no difficulty in retaining the seat by a large majority. A meeting in support of his candidature will be held in St. Barnabas' school on Monday evening, under the presid- ency of Alderman James Evans. In a circular i*sued this week, Mr. Roberts states that he ha a always been strongly in favour 'of every workman being paid, not only a living wage, but something more, in order that he and his family may not merely exist, but be able to live in the best and truest sense of the word. If it had been possible for him to have been present when Councillor Halliwell's motion was discussed by the Town Council, he would have acted consistently with his honest belief and supported the principle of a living wage with all his heart. Mr. S. Gough is standing chiefly as an economist. He asks the Whitecross electors to "vote for S. Gough who will oppose all profit making out of the Corpora- tion. Then you will have a chance of getting cheaper gas, water, electric light and power."

div.head: ORFORD WARD.
div.p: ORFORD WARD.

Mr. J. Halliwell is backed by a most enthusiastic band of Liberal workers and we confidently expect his return on Wednesday next. His action in carrying through the Council ta resolution granting a minimum wage of 245. to all able-bodied workers in the employ of the Corporation is very popular with the electors. Mr. Halliwell also points to his efforts for the ward and to his vote in favour of cheaper bathing facilities. He says he is anxious to see the water rate on baths removed. Mr. Halliwell's opponent is Mr. G. F. Robson, the nominee of the Trades and Labour Council who will hold a meeting in Silver Street School on Monday. ST. JOHN'S WARD.
In this ward Mr. James Hampson,Socialist, is challenging the return of Mr. F. T. Lashford, the retiring Conservative repre- sentative.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
i. The Apple of Eden."

Eleanor Glynn's well known story " Three Weeks " is the foundati,m of the play which is being enacted upon the Royal Court 'Theatre stage this week. It abounds in atrong and romantic situations with highly emotional verbal intercourse between the two characters of the Queen of Slav)nia and Julian Hand- bury, round whose love affairs all the incidents centre. These two impersonations, taken by Miss Doris , Gilham and Mr. Richard Greene respectively, are ' however not quite equally balanced as to the manner of their acting, for while Miss Cilbam is somewhat too emphatic and therefoie lacking in tenderness of ' concepticn of the lot of the unhappy Margaret, Mr. Greene is far tco undemonstrative and phlegmatic a lover to be very convincing in the part of the enamoured Julian. The thankless and somewhat difficult character of the debauched King is taken by Mr. Stephen Scanlan in quite an adequate manner and several others in minor parts are quite satisfactory. The reaction followiog upon last week's crowded houses at San Try" probabl7 accounts for rather meagre audiences during this week. THE ELLEA BAND.

A grand concert of sacred and classical music will te given by the famous Ellery Band on Sunday evening, commencing at eight o'clock. There are no fewer than .7,0 performers in the band. which has a magnificent reputation, and daring the whole of this week has been performing with great success in Liverpool. For to-morrow evening Mr. Chancing illlery has secured the engagement of two splendid singers in Mr. Wallace, tenor, and Mr. Bayne Young, baritone. The latter created a great sensation in Liverpool on Wednesday night. Mr. Young will sing" Dio Possente "from" Faust." The doors will open at Z3O. and atlinitsion will be by pro- grstnine at 23 ,- Is , andtai.

We own that many of our supporters are Conservatives, bat this fact does not make the National Service League a party organisation any more than the fact that many " Die Bards" are suffragists makes Women's Suffrage a party question. We own, too, that many of the Labour party are agair,t as, bat the voting at the recent Pride Unions Congress shows th,t they are less against than they were, and without doubt in our Colonies it is the Labour Party itself which ban already been responsible for the introduction of coin- pulaory military training into Australia and New Zealand, and advocates it in South Africa and Canada.
