div.head: HOSPITALS.
div.p: HOSPITALS.
MR. CROSFIELD QUOTES THE CHANCELLOR IN REPLY TO MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P. [To the Editor of the " Examiner "

Sir,—l find from d.tters which I have received from several prominent citizens of Warrington and from the report of a Deputation app ,inted by the Board of Management of the Warringt in Infirmary to wait upon Mr. Harold Smith, that some apprehension in felt by thoee interested in hospitals as to the probable effect of the Insurance Bill upon the fi !social ponitions of these institutions.

The prints upon which these apprehensions are t based were put by Mr. Rylands when he introduced I the Deputation in the following words : " The Board were disposed to think it likely that '] working men when called uponto subscribe fourpenco p3r week, would become discontented and refuse to I continue having a penny per week voluntarily deducted from their wages for the support of the Infirmary. It was felt that the passing of the Insurance Bill aunt present drawn up, would result, it not in the absolute destruction, at any rate in the serious diminution of that source of income. Probably about half the subscriptions came from manufacturers and employers, and be know that many firms had practically intimated that in view of the burden which most be imposed upon then by the Bill, it would be impossible for them to go on with their voluntary subscriptions, Then if it was thought that the tendency of legislation was to transfer hospitals to the State, the prospect of resolving l-gacies would be minimised, inasmuch as charitably disposed persons would not kayo mein; for the benefit of the State." Later on ha said : " If insured pe:sons were to bs provided with medical treatment which would be paid for under the Bill, the doctors stated that they could not Continue to trait patients free of charge when they went to the Infirmary, on the ground that it ceased to he a charity. If the hospitals had to pay their ,to steffs they would be saddled with an expen- diture which it would be impossible to meet." The resolution of the Medical Board of the Infirmary, e which was also read at the Deputation, was as follows " That the Medical Beard Committee are of opinion that they would be unable to give gratuitous attendance to insured persons in the event of the proposed National Insurance Bill becoming law." The fears of the hospital authorities therefore resolve themselves into the following : - First : That _ workmen would deop their subscriptions to the Infirmary fund in consequence of their having to pay fourpence per week to the Insurance Fund. Secondly: Employees would cease their voluntary subscriptions in consequence of their leaving to pay their quota to the Insur ince Fund. Thirdly : That the legacies viewed ty hospitals would be minimized, because the Bill showed a tendenc; to trans'erring hospitals t e

the State. I find that Mr. Harold Smith in his reply to the Deputation failed ton e t any-one of these points,or to give one gleam of consolation to the gentlemen who were apprehensive of the effect of the Bill on the Infirmary. Indeed he described the meeting as a particularly gloomy one, because the grievances about which the Deputation complained were real, end he did not Eee a solution. He had listened to the Debates in the House of Commons and bad heard grievances rallied but had hever heard an answer to them. Then he went in to find fault with the Bill and alt•mpted t , make political capital out of the coca- aim,. It is very evident either tb it Mr. Harold Smith had not studied the subject, or that he bad wilfully concealed the fact that an important deputa- tion bad waited upon the Chancellor of Exchequer as far hack as July 25th last, representing the B itish Hospitals Association and other important organiza- tions representing such Institutions in all parts of the country. It is a pity that be did not read the Report of the Deputation (which has been officially published) before he met the Warrington deputation, for I venture to think that had he:clone so, he would not have described the situation in such gloomy terms, and would not have been obliged to admit that he saw no solution for the alleged difficulties. I have a copy of this interesting report before me, and I cannot do better than ask you to print extracts from it. Your readers will, I think, agree with me, that they answer the points raised very effectively, and prove that after all these apprehensions are not well founded. The two first points mentioned above were raised by Sir William Cobbett, chairman of the Manchester Royal Infirmary, who had been chosen II a meeting representing 200 hospitals of Great Britafn, to be chairman of the committee to take up the matter With reference to the contributions of the employers Mr. Lloyd George asked Sir William the following question! - Do you really believe that the nob employer of Lbour in your neighbourhood will feel that he is under no obligation to contribute to the hospital because be has to pay half what the German employer pays? Sir William Cobbett: "I do not know about the rich employer. I qnite agree that the large rich firms will have a repugnance to withdraw their suburiptions at first, but the small men will do it, I think, at once." It will be seen that the point with reference to the Ismall employers was dealt with by Mr. Lloyd George later on in his final reply which I will venture to quote below. With reference to the contributions of working men : "Sit William Cobbett said the moment they are called upon to make a compulsory payment they will cease to make a voluntary payment. The Chancellor: But they are paying it no, and they are raying more now. Sir William Cobbett : I know they are, and I appreciate what you say entirely ; hot what I any is, that the moment they are compelled to pay, they will insist upon it that the compulsory payment must cover everything. • The Chancellor : That is very remarkable frame of mind. Sir William Cobbett : It is a very common one. The Chancellor: Ido not think it is, it! may say so —because a man pays less he will contribute lean ! There way be something in that, but it is a very subtle interpretation of human nature, which I cannot quite comprehend. Mr, Lupton : Surely your remarks only apply to people who are actively connected with the friendly societies ? The Chancellor Do you really sorbet:id that on the whole you get much outside those . Mr. Lupton: I am sure we do. Every man in a works who receives more than a certain wage contri- butes Id., and every woman and every by who receives less than no much a week That is where the fu•d comes from. The Chancellor : They contribute because they want the use of the hospitals for accidents. We are not roviding for accidents at all, and if they want to one it for accidents that does not interfere with no. Mr. Lupton: It is contributed really generally in the interests of the hospitals, and not in consegoence of accidents. The Chancellor: You think they will not take • genuine interest in the hospitals in the future? Mr. Lupton : lam very much afraid they will not The Chancellor: I really cannot comprehend it. First of all, deal with the six millions of people who are paying now • they will pay less in future for the same benefits. home of them will pay something like half if they have been paying in a friendly society for 10 or 15 years, because their accumulated funds are released. Becau-e they are paying less to their friendly society, because the employer is paying compulsorily, and the State is bringing in its 2d., and therefore they are released to that extent, therefore I urn told they will not contribute to the hospital. There ins second class who, at the present moment, do not leleng to friendly aocieties, but, who being thrifty. persona, still take an interest in the hospitals—a genuine interest in the hospitals, an unselfish one. I am asked to believe—a purely unselfish, philanthropic interest in hospitals. I can well understand that. But because there is a national system of insurance, these people who take a philanthropic interest in hospitals, will cease to take it. Ido not understand it ; I really do not! I thought I knew something of human nature, but this frameof mind is far beyond my compreb ensioo. Mr. Sydney Holland : At the London Hospital we do not get very much from the organised subscriptions of working men; but lam quite certain that employers who are compelled to pay this insurance will cease to subecribe. If the hospitals are not wanted, they must go under. The Chancellor If they ere not wanted, certainly they ought to go under ; but why should they be less Rented under a system of national insurance ? Mr. Sydney Holland : I think hospitals will be wonted just as much, or rather more. The Chancellor : That is exactly what I say." After further conversation with reference to the insurance of hospital employees—a point upon which the Chancellor of the Exchequer made important con- cessions as will be seen from his reply—Mr. Lloyd- George answered the deputation as follows , " %Neil, gentlemen, I am very glad that you have come. I wanted to have an interview with those who are competent to speak en behalf of the hospitals of the country, aid who commanded the confidence of the hospitals if the country. I think you are labouring under apprehensions which you will find will not be justified by the result. You fear that as the result of Ibis Act your anbscriptions will considerably diminish. I do not think there is any reasonable ground to appre- hend that coneeip core. Is 'Laura the workingcl•sree will pay iells than they have hithertea paid, no far as

rtembers of friendly sccieties are concerned, t,reards their friendly eociaties. It will be a relief to there of anything between GI and Is. a month. Tharefore,there is no reason why they shoold not contribute more in the future. Coming to the other classes of the com- munity, I do not believe that moo will neglect their duty towards hospitals because you are calling upon the:a to make a contribution towards sickness amongst . . .

their employees. Ido not believe they will ; Ido sot think that is compatible at all with what we know of human nature. I think you will find there may be a momentary irritation. That always happens whenever you have got any Bill which calls upon people to pay money. I bastard it two or three yews ago, 1 was told there would be no more money coming into the hospitals ; and I was very glad to hear from Sir William that, as the result of the canvass in his neighbourhood, contributions are flowing in at the rate of at least en additional LI 8 a week. Sir William Cobbett . Before the 818 came in. The Chancellor: I know, but it WWI after the other Bill, which I was told was going to dry up all sources of charity. That is really what Jumpers with every- thing that is ever introduced into this House that makes people pay. You always hear there is an end of hospitals, there is an end of all charities, and in (Ware nobody would contribute anything towards scything. Human nature is much better than it likes to represent itself, as a matter of fact •, and after the momentary irritation passes, people will do their duty towards charities end towards every other Institution in the same sort of way. I am simply dealing with apprehensions which I think are exaggerated, and naturally exaggerated. You fear for the great Institut ions which have bean worked up through years sod generations of labour, of toil, of sicritioe, and of anxiety. Yoe are naturally apt rebore. sive lest something should be carried through this House of Commons that will destroy the great work which you heve devoted your lives to building up. I am not at all complaining of that ; I think it ins very natural anxiety on your part; hut I do not think you will Rod it will be justified by the sequel. I come now to the next point. Supposing you found °were so, that the hospitals were impoverished, that the sources of subscription were dried up, the hospitals of this country are so essential a part of the machinery of civilisation that! cannot imagine any country allow- ing a single hospital to be closed. I am perfectly certain they will not. Ido not went to indicste at the present moment what would have to be done, but I am perfectly clear in my own mind veutt would have to be done. No Government could possibly allow hospitals to be closed, because they were short t•f mush to carry on their work. But if I were to indicate it at the present moment, that would certainly be a n•ore effective way of stopping subscriptions than anything that is con- tiated is this Bill, Rod therefore, I do not want to dwell upon that. All I con say is that no Government can allow a. single hospital to be closed, because,! again repeat, it is tart of the essential machinery of civilisation in any country. In Germany, as I have already pointed out, the hospital system has developed and grown and strengthened since the Insurance Bill was brought in, because it educates public opinion as to the need for hospitals, and as to the important part they play in healing ; and that is more important for hospitals than almost anything you can imagine in order to induce people to subscribe towards them. Mr. Sydney Holland complains that we have not legislated for hospitals. It is for the vary reason which was urged by Sir Savile Crossley. It is because we believe in the voluntary system, anal we want it to continue. If we started legislating for hospitals and handed fends over to hospitals, that would mean con- trol over hospitals, and the voluntary system would be at an end for ever. But you cannot have it both ways. If you want to he put upon the fund, you must be put upon the fund on the same conditions as any other institution which is on the fund—on the condition that there is a certain measure of Government control over your work. Here Too are In complete command of the situation. If patients are sent to you who are upon the insurance fund. without an adequate contribution from those funds you are in the position to say," We cannot take them unless you are prepared to meet us." You are free contracting parti s, and I think you are in a position to say to the approved societies in future, when they see getting a contribution from the State and forced contributions from the employers, You really must help us along." Ire you are living s hand-to-mouth existence ; you have got to go cap in hand and beg for contributions for work that ought to be a public obligation; therefore, I think, your position will really be considerably strengthened under the Bill. Under clause 12—I am rather surprised you have not called attention to that • —a suggestion has been made to me, end it is a 'ogees- Hon which I am considering, whether is certain oases the sick pay eta p,..,rron who bad no dependent shonld not, where he is a charge upon the hoapital, in some form or other be a subscription te the hospital itself. That is worth considerirg. I am not inn position at the present moment to give you any answer up-a it: but that would undoubtedly very considerably strengthen the fleanciel position of the hospitals themselves. It is a difficult business. We are really trying to do our best for the notional health. We are raising enormous sums of money for the purpose. Everybody. without distinction of party, said this must be done ; but the Moment you attempt to do it, everybody has his own individual grievances and raises difficulties. I am not complaining of that ; but at the mime time I should be glad to find out where this 15 millionsof money is supposed to be going, bemuse I have not dis- covered anybody yet who is receiving it. We are raising just 15 millions of money, and I find everybody thinks they are worse off than they were before. That cannot be the case. I should be very much obliged if it were possible for you to talk the matter over with the medics! profession, sad then to come to rate with some sort of arrangement with regeral to these cases which come to the hospital and which are taken off their bands. I do not know that 1 conli carry it any further at the present moment. I will consider very carefully all the suggestions which you have made ; some of them I think I shall be able to meet, and the other ones! shall hope to make earn, progr ass with. It will therefore be seen that the answers to the three points raiaed are : First : It is very unlikely that the working men of the country who, generally speaking, are moat honourable in their dealings, will, in view of the fact that they are paying eightpence per month less to their Friendly Societies, discontinue their contiibu- lions of oie psnny plc week to the hospitals. They will really be in a better position to contribute be these Institutions than they have ever been. It seems to me that if they male any change at all work- ing men would be more likely to increase than to diminish their contributions. Secondly: Experience proves that threats of reduct:on of subicriptilne to charities by employers of labour and other capitalists whilst any piece of legislation is going through Parliament are never carried into effect, as Mr. Lloyd-George says— 'human nature ia always much better than it likes to represent itself."

Thirdly The Bill does not in any respect propose to put hospitals on the State. Therefore, the appre- hension with reference to minimized legacies is not well grounded. Fourthly : Provisions am to be made in the Bill by which hospitals may receive the merUcal benefit of csrt3ln in-ps.ients which they treat. This wets the objection of the doctors who stated that they would not continue to trait insured patients free of charge. Lastly: The resoltrion of the Medical Board is met by the fact that insured psrson, will receive full medical benefit under the National Insurance Bill, and that therefore that Board will not be called upon to give gratuitous attendance, to such persons. I trust that the Hospital Authorities in Warrington and throughout the country, swill in consideration of these fasts realise that so far from the Insurance Bill being calculated to prejudice their interests, it is I believe going to be great factor in malting more perfect the work which these insti titions have so magnificendy car, ied out in the past.—Yours A. It CILOSFIELD,

div.head: EMPIRE SKATING HALL.
div.p: EMPIRE SKATING HALL.

A large number of peop'e have again made use of the opportunities of enjoyment afforded by the Empire Skating Rink. Last Saturday evening considerably over 490 persons donned the akatee and spun round to the merry strains produced by the orchestra. On Thursday evening a juvenile fancy dress carnival took place and besides there being a great comber of skaters there were more spectators than usual. The children were attired in various costumes, some of them bewitching and faseinatieg by their charming appear- ance and others humorous and original. Valuable prizes were awarded and for these there was keen competition.

div.head: SEQUEL TO MOTOR ACCIDENT
div.p: SEQUEL TO MOTOR ACCIDENT
Provision Dealer Suet.

At the Warrington County Court on 'Thursday before his Honour Judge H. V. Stanger, IC C. the case was resumed in which Allston hloriand Johnsen, electrical engineer, Manchester, claimed .£l2 131. 3.1. for personal injuries and damages to a motor cycle, alleged to have been sustaieed by the negligent driving of a motor cat by .1. Bayley Isaac, provision dealer, ‘Narrington. Mr. Suffer, of Blanchester (instructed by Mr. 1%. 11. Todd, Manchester), appeared fo• the plaintiff, and Mr. Cuthbert Smitb, of Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. Wood and L-ird. Manchesteri for the defendant. The case for the plaintiff was that when Le was cycling from Chester to Manchester on Whitsunday defendant's car da,hed out of the Tarporley— Warrington-road and he was entrapped. He swerved to the left but the ear knocked him down. The defeatist also tried to avoid the collision but he was going at too great a speed to enable him to pull up. The motor car made an effort to turn to the right and in doing so collided with the porch of an old toll house, broke one of the pillars and also demoliehed part of the structure itself. The .plaintiff gave evidence and, in reply to Mr Smith, deeied that he admitted after LI" accident that it was his fault the accident occurred. The evidence for the defence stas thst the born of the motor car was sounded and that the plaintiff was going at such a speed that he could not avoid running into them. The car was travelling at between 4 and .; miles an hour. The case was adjourned until November 23rd.

div.head: CONTEMPT OF COURT.
div.p: CONTEMPT OF COURT.
Judge Rebukes Warrington Traveller.

At the Warrington County Court, on Tbureday William DPNeil Sloane, formerly a traveller in the employ of Messrs Orme and Sons, billiard table makers, Manchester, •ppeared before bin llonourJudge Stanger to answer an order of attachment for contempt of court issued by his Honour a fortnight ago for not haying delivered up, as ordered, a railway contract rind • Manchester Royal Exchange membership ticket. Sloane explained to his lionour that when he received the 611M11/008 be had made an application for s situation at Leeds, and he was still under LI 0 impression that the railway contract was his property, so one bad been given to him for the part live or 911 years as a Christ- mas gift. He had also been ill. His Honour pointed out that by Sloane having retained the ticket his former employers were prevented from receiving any benefit on the surrender value or getting it transferred to someone else. If be disagreed with the judgment of the court, he ought to have brought an action in another court to have it set aside. As longs. the judgment was not net aside, it was bind- ing and ought to have been obeyed. Sloane said he was extremely sorry he had disobeyed the order of the court. People did things which they. did not think wrong et the time. His Honour tail there was a forther complaint. Sloane did not appear in court • fortnight ego and only sent a letter with the ticket. just tefore the Ccurt commenced. He most mate an order against him for the costs of the application. Slosne said ha had not got a shilling of his own to pay any costs. He had dine no 'nor, since !lay ASO bad • wife and family depending upon biro. His Honour said the mitten was a very serious one, and ha must take tima to coral ler his decision. The only semblance of explanation that Sloane had made was that he had been ill. It was gross contempt of court, and su..b conduct could not brit tolerated. Before the rising of the Con t Skase again appeared before the Judge who said that the offence hi. had committed was. very grave one and if such things were allowed order would Le reduced to chaos. Sloane repeated that he was very sorry sad that at the time he was ill. The dodge said that in vine of that he would canuel the order sod allow defendant to go.

A great International and Universal Exhibition will be held in Ghent, the Manchester of Belgium, In 1913. The object of this announcement is to urge the British Manufacturer to make a show worthy of cur great Empire ard to remember that the ancient battle ground of Europe has now become the one neutral ground where the Inter- national Market can be made a success, as German and French alike will come to Ghent to see and buy our wares. The Exhibition Department of the Board of Trade has been approached to assure an adequate participation for England next to the French section. Germany will have an admirable display and our Manufacturers must not neglect this opportunity. The Exhibition will be bigger than the Brussels 1910 and the w hole will be on. scale of magnificence hitherto unknown. It is under the direct Patronage of H.M. King Albert.
